In this era of mechanized power no nation, however strong, can hope to stand alone. We recognize that the ideal of world peace is comparatively new. Nation has warred with nation since the beginning of time, and periods of no war have been very few and scattered. But the ideal is here, and I feel that the League of Nations moved us just a little bit closer to that ideal. The league was meant to control war, and what a world it started out in! Of the seven great powers, the United Kingdom, with the dominions and France, were the only two who belonged to it throughout the years. The United States never belonged, and Russia went through the throes of a bloody revolution and its aftermath. Italy was very soon dominated by a man who preached war as an instrument of international policy. Germany belonged for a few short years, and Doctor Stresemann's death was a tragedy for us all. I do not think that Japan ever understood any of the principles that underlay the League of Nations and what it hoped to do in the score of years that intervened between these two great wars. Yet even now there are nineteen nations paying dues to the League of Nations, and the International Labour Organization.
I wish to quote from a statement of June 15 of this year, by Mr. P. G. Waterson of the League of Nations, of Princeton, where one of the divisions of the league is still in exile, just as the International Labour Office is here in Montreal. With regard to the payment of dues this is what 'he says:
During the course of 1942 the following countries made contributions: Australia. Belgium, Canada, Chile, Czechoslovakia, Egypt, France, Ireland, India, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, the Union of South Africa, United Kingdom.
I have not as yet received full information regarding the present year but believe the payments have also been received from Mexico and Portugal. In the above I have not included states members of the international labour organization but not members of the league. The regular payers among them comprise the United States of America, Brazil, Chile, Venezuela. In addition, the United States of America also contribute to the league in respect of their participation in the work of the opium section.
That is signed by Mr. P. G. Waterson. These countries therefore must see a hope even yet in the league, and we may yet build on what has survived of that league ideal. We do not know what form the new peace treaties will take, but here is evidence of willingness to cooperate in the attempt to bring peace and security and order out of chaos through a collective system. I am /Mrs. Casseiman.]
not arguing for a renewal of the league in the form in which it stood. It is still too early to make any blueprints. The war itself will shape the future, will create and harden international relationships. There is a tremendous outpouring of hate now against Germany in the occupied countries. Why would there not be? Contemptuous, coldblooded, calculated cruelty must engender hate. But on the other hand I do not think there has ever been such good-will among some of the powers of the world that are now allied as there is at the present time; and after all, good-will is a pretty good basis for any international cooperation.
I wonder if we could capitalize on that good-will now. Could we not, while the realization of what we owe is strong upon us, begin to shape that cooperation now? I believe it is being shaped quietly and efficiently, through such negotiations as the Prime Minister has put before us. Let me indicate the desire for cooperation. Take the British empire, or the commonwealth, whichever you call it. Do you not think that our allies are more friendly now than they were back in 1938 and 1939? They now see the issues at stake which they did not see in 1939. They have seen the British people stand up alone after the defeat of France to take tremendous punishment with unbowed heads and fearless hearts. Do not more people now realize the truth in the words of General Smuts when, referring to the empire, he said:
This greatest human experiment in political organization, this precedent and anticipation of what one hopes may be in store for human society in years to come.
It is not that we think the commonwealth has failed that we advocate a wider order. Surely our allies see that British imperialism is a thing of the past.
What about Russia? Has there ever been a time in the last quarter of a century when Russia's stock stood higher? We have evidence that Russia's suspicions of her allies are much less to-day than they have been at any time in the last quarter of a century. That may be shown by the twenty-year pact of friendship between Great Britain and Russia, and by Russia's recent dissolution of the Comintern. One of the ways by which Russia thought she might bring about better conditions for everybody in all the countries in the world was through the communist idea. It was revolution in Russia and world revolution, in theory. In France, before its fall, its last parliament contained I believe seventy communist members. But the Russian nation has dissolved the Comintern as if it now

War Appropriation-External Affairs
thought that there might be better ways of collaborating than through a revolution. Russia's stock stands high.
What about China? We know now what China learned years ago, the strength and barbarity of Japan. The British, like the Chinese, have stood up under the bombing of their cities. A new bond there! We must hold fast to the comradeship which has been established in the face of the common enemy and the common danger.
In the United States we find a new realization of her position and responsibility as a great power. This is shown in the public utterances of President Roosevelt and other outstanding men. I quote just this one paragraph from a speech made in April of this year by Sumner Welles:
And I am even more convinced that unless the American people are willing to assume their fair share of responsibility for the maintenance of peace in the world of the future, by joining in the exercise of powers when they may be determined by international agreement to be necessary, and by participating in such other forms of international cooperation as may effectively prevent the rise of economic or political dangers, the peace of the world cannot be maintained.
Take the state legislatures. A report in the press of July 3 states that in thirteen of the legislatures of the United States resolutions have been introduced and agreed upon to the effect that they are convinced that the sequence to victory in this world war must be international organization of all nations to lay the foundations of peace. These resolutions differ from one state to another, but thirteen legislatures of the United States have adopted such a resolution. Those states are: North Carolina, New Jersey, Montana, Maryland, New York, Vermont, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, Alabama and Florida.
It may also have been noticed that the Republican party, somewhat isolationist but not entirely, has set up the Republican Postwar Policy Association, which according to the press is making international collaboration a part of its programme.
What about our other allies? The mutilated, occupied nations of Europe, some of which were neutral back in the first great war, have a different idea now I think of how closely they should collaborate. We have all realized that we cannot have the benefit of national sovereignty in its entirety and at the same time enjoy security.
Our other allies of the Americas have shown that they realize what it is all about. They have shown it by their membership in the League of Nations, and by the joint accord they signed in January, 1942, in Washington. 72537-2941
I maintain that never before in the last twenty-five years has there been a time when there has been a better basis for action based upon good-will among the allied nations of the world to bring about a system out of which we may hope to attain peace and security. Not that good-will alone can give us peace and security; that is only part of it. But it is a good basis. You must have the institutions through which that good-will can act. But the war (has taught us the alternative to collaboration among the countries of the world, and the alternative is another war, I believe, within the century.
Making the peace will bristle with difficulties. Let no one imagine that it can be easily done. In spite of mutual respect there will be an aftermath of bitterness and of disillusionment which may nullify the best efforts of our statesmen. Statesmen are only human, with the weaknesses and strengths to which human nature is subject. Will the democracies stand by their statesmen? You know the dangers there. National leaders at peace negotiations know that back home millions of people are watching to see that there is no sacrifice of national prestige or national sovereignty. The elected president or the elected prime minister knows how easily political opponents seize on every opportunity to denounce any concessions made. That is why we so desperately need an informed public opinion which will steadily hold up the hands of our statesmen. One does not need to go far afield to get examples of leaders who were not followed. But I did go far afield and I have here a quotation from an article by Doctor F. W. Sollmann, who was a member of the German government in 1923, an associate of Stresemann and editor of a chain of papers under Kaiser Wilhelm. He was one of the German delegates to Versailles in 1919, and fled from Germany in 1933 since when he lias been a resident of Pennsylvania. He makes this statement in an article in the Dalhousie Review for May entitled "Facing the German people":
Chancellor Stresemann often told me how he suffered under unfair attack in his own party. He and the first Reich president of the republic, Frederick Ebert, and many statesmen, died prematurely, hunted down by the attacks of a slandering opposition.
I went far afield for that.
The only hope of avoiding the danger of the demagogue's appeal is an informed public opinion. Extremists are always vocal. Can we in Canada understand that foreign relations must be removed from the realm, of partisan party politics if stable relations with

War Appropriation-External Affairs
other nations are to be built up? How can we reconcile our democratic right of criticism with steady support of international policy? Preparation for peace should mean the awareness of our own people of the sacrifices that must be made for peace. An informed public opinion, yes, and how can it become informed? Years of study will still leave much to be desired, but we should know something of the difficulties which come through the clash in national objectives. I think we ought to realize that the basis of lack of cooperation is a fear of domination, a fear that somebody else will form your policy for you. If we are ever to arrive at collaboration we must realize that other nations feel the same way about these things as we do. Let us not forget, when we speak of democratic countries, that the German people voted Hitler into power, mainly because he promised the easy way to get rid of mass unemployment, and to place Germany in the sun again. They voted him into power, and every democratic country faces a like possibility unless we have an informed public opinion that can examine policies from a non-partisan angle as they are set before them.
I should like to read a quotation from the Christian Science Monitor. This is an editorial which appeared on Armistice day, 1942. It might be entitled "How far can we go in collaboration?"
To-day the problem of durable peace is being discussed from so many angles that the public is in danger of confusion. If, before we can have peace, the income of every person must be guaranteed, if every vestige of racial or social discrimination must be obliterated, if every man must adhere to rules which mortals have never learned completely to live by, then peace is indeed a complicated business, and not to be achieved short of a perfect world.
That may be true of the peace that passeth all understanding; it is not true of the peace that exists between states joined in federal union, or which are members of a commonwealth, or which have recognized their fundamental interests as bound up with other nations. Among such peoples political peace is preserved by sharing in maintenance of forces protecting order while justice is being won. The next goal for world peacemakers may well be the establishment of this concept of sharing a single force for the preservation of world order. As much justice as is possible of achievement must of course be written into the next peace, but the supreme aim is that the peace shall be protected by force as widely supported as possible.
I should like to read what Anthony Eden said about this century in an address he made on July 3 to the English-speaking union in London. He said he was more than ever convinced that "the message of the twentieth century is the utter interdependence of all nations."

There is much more that I should like to say. This is pretty much theory, but you have to have theory before you can do anything elsA You require support for a policy that is to be put into force. I am very much interested in this question of peace and war;
I am concerned as all people are because war makes or breaks a nation and the civilization of the world. We must build together with other nations if we hope to build a permanent structure.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that we listened with some interest and perhaps with some expectation to the Prime Minister's speech of last Friday on foreign policy. I was, however, a little disappointed to discover that within about half an hour the Prime Minister spent some considerable time in reviewing the world situation as it appears to-day, making special reference to the war in the Pacific; he spent some time on the recently conducted food conference, and on the question of refugees from Europe, and therefore in the half hour period there was not much time left for him to give to this country the foreign policy of his government for the next year. It has become almost the rule of the day for the government to say this and that is a matter of government policy; therefore we cannot announce it until the appropriate time-the appropriate time meaning when the government thinks it is appropriate.
May I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we are passing estimates for the year 1943-44. We are asked to vote sums of money for the administration of the Department of External Affairs to carry on some sort of policy for the next year; therefore when we are being asked to vote appropriations for the ensuing year the country has a right to know what the government's foreign policy is for that year, and so far as I am concerned-and I think the whole house will agree-we are still at a loss to know what that policy is. I believe I could go a little further and suggest that last Friday's debate, and the debate that is now in progress can be regarded as a continuation of it, is perhaps one of the most important debates that has taken place in parliament this year. That has been referred to before, and I thought that all parties of the house would take the opportunity to announce what their foreign policy might be. But I have not heard in any very pronounced terms what the foreign policy of the Progressive Conservative party is. I happen to have in my files a printed document which came out of the Winnipeg convention, I believe. It is entitled "Freedom, security, opportunity and

War Appropriation-External Affairs
the British partnership policy of the Progressive Conservative party." They do not have a great deal to say about it, although they go a little farther than the Prime Minister went on Friday. The Prime Minister did not tell us what the policy of his government was in respect of future foreign relations.
I come now to the next speaker, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I expected that he would announce what the foreign policy of his party was, but I listened in vain. He spent some considerable time justifying a statement he made in respect of the appointment of one of our foreign representatives, and some little time in respect of the Jewish refugee question, but I listened in vain for a pronouncement with regard to their foreign policy. I happen to have with me an article which I cut out of Canadian Business. This article has to do with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I find there are six points enumerated, but I cannot see anything with regard to their foreign policy. Statements which have been made in the past indicate to me that there is one tribute I might well pay to their late leader, Mr. Woodsworth, and that is that he was indeed a sincere and honest man, and that he was candid in his pronouncements in the house. My memory goes back to a time only a few short years ago when he sat in the house, and I recall clearly that on every occasion on which foreign policy was discussed his voice was heard. I do not know that the policy of that party has changed, but pronouncements which have been made in the past would lead one to the belief that their policy, in a word, is one of internationalism. There have been a few statements which would indicate that they are not particularly definite in respect of Canada's policy in the British commonwealth of nations, but they do seem to be definite in respect of collective security of some kind. I always have asked myself the question: Collective security with whom? So far as I am concerned there is no greater collective security in the whole world than that embodied in the British commonwealth of nations. The other day the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), stated something which has great value in respect of our attitude on foreign policy. Following that up I shall read only a few sentences from a speech by the hon. member for Yegreville (Mr. Hlynka), on February 18, 1943, where at page 521 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
To me the British crown is the heart and symbol of the British commonwealth of free and sovereign peoples. To me the British crown is the symbol of unity and the heritage of British ideals of more than a thousand years. More than that, we should prize our position
within the commonwealth because we are the benefactors in all and everything that has been achieved over centuries of progress. For instance, should it not occur to us that we are equal partners in a unique association of free sovereign nations. . . . Let me point out the underlying principles of our British democratic system. It is simply this, that the extent and the power of the British commonwealth of nations are consistent with the maximum of individual freedom, the maximum of local and provincial autonomy, and the maximum of sovereignty of each unit-nation, fitting into the pattern of the commonwealth. This philosophy of statecraft has been built on practical experience, and it is opposed to other philosophies which are supported by many, and which include the surrender of our national sovereignty in favour of some super state. ... The philosophy of the British people is diametrically opposite to that of totalitarianism in whatever form it appears.
The greatest assurance of individual freedom that can be found is expressed in those principles underlying the crown of the British commonwealth of nations. And to surrender any of that sovereignty to an outside body, and work from the top down to the people, is the very converse of democracy. Democracy, first and foremost, is the freedom of the individual expressing itself to its government and its administration. It is government exercising its powers to bring into existence the results that the will of the people desire. The setting up of international institutions does not guarantee that individual freedom. I do not say of course that there should not be some measure or some programme of international cooperation. International cooperation is one thing, but internationalism that will give over any of our national sovereign rights to a central power outside ourselves is neither democratic nor tending to assure individual freedom.
I do not know that we can properly diagnose the present world situation by simply looking at things as they appear on the surface. I am reminded of a solemn and striking portion of holy writ which says:
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
That is true. Hidden somewhere in behind the scenes of human activity the forces of evil which operate backstage are the forces to be most feared. I suggest that the present world conflict, after all, becomes only an incident in the progress of history. What are we fighting for in this war? That question is often asked. It is usually answered by stating what we are fighting against, and we are usually told that we are fighting against the totalitarianism of Europe, that we stand for democracy, and that our fight is against totalitarianism with all its evils. It seems

to me the dangerous situation is that in fighting against the evil powers of totalitarianism abroad, Canada and the other countries of the British commonwealth of nations may find themselves in the grip of a state-dominated system of our own making, because of powers which operate behind the scenes for eventual world domination. I am convinced that there are very powerful forces at work to bring about this disastrous condition. This is evidenced by bold assertions coming from many quarters that instead of a reconstructed democratic order after the war we must expect more government control, more bureaucratic regimentation, and all the other odious features of totalitarianism which have created so much havoc in Europe.
Much of that might be taking place in our own country, right under our own noses. But what of the world at large? I am not apologizing to the Prime Minister for saying this, but I think he should have stood up on Friday night and told the world that as far as Canada is concerned we will never countenance any move toward a supranational or world government, or any other move or utterance that would ask the people of Canada to give up any part of their sovereignty. If he had said that, I think he would have received the plaudits of this nation. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said that Canada needs the British empire-I agree with him. He said that the British empire needs Canada-I agree with him. I would go further and say that the world needs the British empire. I am convinced that there are powers that are seeking to destroy that empire, and have been for years. I am convinced that what took place in the two decades before the war was nothing more than a move on the part of unseen powers to render helpless the British commonwealth of nations.
May I say something which has been said before-this thought was expressed this morning by the hon. member for Lethbridge-I think it is nothing short of a miracle that Great Britain withstood the enemy in those years gone by. Dunkirk was a miracle, and it is a miracle that Great Britain, the British commonwealth of nations, and Canada too, have in such a short time come to be such powerful nations in respect to armaments. It is a miracle that this has been done, and perhaps the hand of Providence had something to do with it.
I have a good deal of material in my scrapbook, and I could not help but turn up a certain article a few days ago when that wonderful lady, Madame Chiang Kai-shek, was here. We applauded her, we praised the great
[Mr. Hansell.)
courage of the Chinese people, and we listened to her with all the intensity of our souls. It was a great day in Canadian history when she spoke in this chamber, but while I listened to her I could not help but hang my head in shame as I thought of what had happened in days gone by when the British commonwealth of nations was powerless to help China against the onslaught of powerful militaristic Japan. I went up to my office and I turned up an article which had been written by Madame Chiang Kai-shek and which appeared in Liberty magazine of December, 1940. This was over a year after the war had started. I should like to read just a few paragraphs from the pen of Madame Chiang Kai-shek. This is not someone else reporting Madame Chiang Kai-shek; it is what she wrote herself. She said:
Japan's easy conquest of Manchuria by unscrupulous means was but an example of how an aggressor could safely kick irksome principles into limbo and survive unscathed to enjoy not only the possessions of the "conquered" territory, but also the continued political, economic, and social good-will and friendship of those democratic nations which were originally the most vociferous in their denunciation of the aggression. Japan had tested international reactions to undeclared warfare, to the wholesale abrogation of treaties; and she found them empty of danger-either immediate or remote.
Have we reason to believe that any supranational authority can bring about treaties which will be any more sound? The article continues;
When Japan invaded Manchuria we refrained from resisting because the League of Nations undertook to adjust matters. They lost the region for us. There was a difference, however, when the Japanese proceeded to invade China proper. Then we abandoned faith in international undertakings, and we fought. For more than three years now Japan has been gouging with ferocious intensity at the very vitals of our country. She set the example for the wholesale slaughter and destruction now running riot in Europe-an example that might never have materialized had the democracies only fulfilled their obligations to China by restraining Japan.
Without the League of Nations.

She says that the League of Nations broke down, that they were not able to handle the situation, that they were powerless. She goes on to refer to the power of money, the power of cartels-she does not use that word here-and the power of world trade. She refers to the fact that the great democracies were feeding Japan with munitions of war but were not doing the same thing for China. The article continues:
America amassed profits by selling to Japan the necessities of warfare. Eighty per cent of Japan's war supplies came from America-

And Canada.

She said that eighty per cent came from America; I can only quote what is written here. The article continues:
[DOT]-and ninety-five per cent of the aviation gasoline which was used by Japan in her ruthless bombing was American.
China has thus been compelled to fight a war not of her own making with a power which has been aided and abetted unstintingly by the markets of the democracies. These markets were virtually closed to us, for no help was given us to avail ourselves of them. China has been the champion of the principles for which other democracies are now at war, but mention of what China has been able to do for the cause is seldom if ever made-an amazing situation.
And further:
What has happened, however-and what has not happened-is another great lesson to the Chinese people, another bitter lesson that they will never forget. They will remember never to believe in international promises, no matter how many imposing seals adorn the documents.
And again:
What the future holds no one can tell, of course. If, unhappily, for the democracies as well as for China, we should be defeated in the end, at least the world ought to know that we w-ere beaten not because of lack of courage -either moral or physical

but because China was strangled to death by an economic noose fashioned by Japan out of British appeasement, American profiteering, and French fear.
There is one thing I should like to say in that respect. It was not the people of China, or the people of Canada, the United States or Great Britain, who had anything to do with that. The governments were responsible. Once again I refer you to that passage of holy writ which says:
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
The hidden hand of world finance is at work to destroy humanity and civilization, if possible, and one of the best ways it can do it is by destroying the British commonwealth of nations; and one of the pieces of ingenuity, I personally believe, wrought by that hidden hand is to set up a supranational world government which will have control of a world monetary unit which will in turn control if possible the internal economy of every nation in the world, the British empire included. The Prime Minister would have done a service to himself and his government had he stood up here on Friday and said, "This government will never tolerate the handing over of our sovereignty to any internationalism, no matter by what name it may be called."
This is a time in the world's history when the foreign policy of this country should be announced. It is a time in the history of this
country when the Prime Minister should promise the Canadian people that no commitments shall be made and no documents embodying such commitments shall be signed until those commitments are known to this parliament, and through parliament to the people, so that the people themselves can say "yes" or "no" regarding those commitments. But, knowing what has happened, I can suggest what is going to happen. I do not know who will represent us at the peace conference, but I am sure that a number of significant things will happen before the conference. Diplomats will be running all over the place. In his speech on Friday the Prime Minister mentioned certain international conferences. I doubt whether we know what goes on there behind the scenes. I do not say that the Prime Minister should be so bold as to tell the whole world, but it is the right of the people's representatives to know from A to Z what goes on behind those closed doors, and he can tell us in a secret session if he wishes to do so. These events are happening while the people's minds are occupied with the war. The technique of evil powers seems to be to get the people's minds off the future and keep them on what is happening to-day, confuse them with this and that, worried as they are with the fate of their loved ones battling overseas, so that these evil powers can put over their designs now. I believe I can see what is going to happen. I do not know who will sit at the peace table; it may be the Prime Minister; certainly it will not be myself or any member of our group; I doubt very much whether it will be any members of the party to my right.
What about us?

I do not know whether the Progressive Conservative party will gain much power. The fact is that we do not know what is the Prime Minister's policy of the future, in relation either to foreign affairs or to domestic politics. I fear that commitments will be made, that documents will be signed, and that this parliament will be asked not what it wishes to do, but to ratify commitments which have already been made. If I am in parliament at that time I may have the privilege of reminding hon. members of this prediction.
I can only reiterate that I believe the Prime Minister owes it to Canada to give us, before the debate is ended, a full pronouncement upon his government's foreign policy.

speechtext:
I have one or two words to say after the speech made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) this morning, and I am grasping this early opportunity of doing so.
The hon. member referred this morning to statements which he said I had made at some occasion or another. I asked him then if he could produce any such statements. He said he was looking for them and he hoped to be able to produce them. I notice that he has been back in the chamber since, and he has not taken advantage of the opportunity of producing them, so that I assume he has not found them. It would have been generous, of course, to say that he had not found them, because no such documents can be shown to exist, but since he has not cared to do that, I should take this opportunity of saying that there is nothing whatever in the assertions he made and that no such documents or statements can be found because they do not exist. In fact the one thing he specifically referred to, namely the manifesto which he said was published in the Winnipeg Free Press, was not only not signed by me-it was signed by a very considerable number of distinguished Canadians, including a number of Conservatives

but also it did not bear anything of the import ascribed to it. This manifesto is a declaration of Canadian unity in war and peace, and it urged that the Canadian government and parliament should put itself on record, before an occasion presented itself when it would have to declare war or not, that it had the right to do so. I remember being asked to sign this at the time, and I refused to sign it for two reasons. The first of those two reasons was that I did not think the time was ripe for it. I thought that at that time, when war seemed imminent, the document would be misunderstood-which I may say was the reason given by the Prime Minister for rejecting the legislation it advocated. Second, I felt that the course that would be pursued by the parliament and government of Canada would establish the course that was advocated and would make the point abundantly clear, as I thought it should be made in the interests of the unity of Canada and of our greatest possible contribution to the cause which at that time everyone could see lay ahead.
May I say just one or two other words on the same point. When the hon. member for York-Sunbury said that I should not have said that I advocated one British statesman in opposition to another, I admit his charge completely: I should not have said it, and I never did make that advocacy in public. I
[Mr. Hansell.)
did however feel provoked by the attitude of some people to the views I then expressed. Events have justified the views I then expressed. However, I should not have said that to the house, because I never made that advocacy in public, and probably it would have been improper for me to do so.
In all this discussion there seems to be a fundamental confusion, which is so extraordinary as to be almost deliberate, between a point of view which was one of simple self-respect in Canada, and what the hon. member for York-Sunbury calls isolationism. I venture to say that if you look back over the record-and I can give the texts of all the speeches I have made, which are far too many

from 1932 on, you will find that there has been no more determined anti-isolationist in Canada than myself. You will see too that the veiy commencement of my taking any active part in the discussion of external affairs was my strong antipathy to the policy then being taken by the government of which the hon. member for York-Sunbury was a member. That policy was taken at Geneva in 1932. It was expressed by my predecessor in this house in a speech which he delivered at Geneva on I think December 12, 1932, and it was a policy which was then generally regarded by most students of the subject as one that was not strongly opposed to the position and the pretensions of Japan with regard to Manchuria. With that policy I disagreed, and I believe that events have proved the attitude I then took right, because it was that policy and the kind of thing it represented which led to the deterioration of international affairs everywhere.
Would the hon. member be a little more specific regarding that policy? We are interested to know what policy he upholds.

It was a policy of acquiescence in the attitude taken by Japan with regard to the conquest by force of a part of China. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a long statement involving quite a few assertions of what my hon. friend takes to be facts, but I should say that if there was one stage in the history of the world when the nations did have the strength required to make a stand it was then, if they had been willing to use it. The fact is that they were not willing to use it -not all of them. I am only led on to this -I nope my hon. friends will recognize it- because I do not believe in isolation and I have never believed in it. I believe that every step where we have gone wrong from 1920 to date has been due to failure on the part, not of this government but of most governments to live up to their obligations. Of course, Canada cannot take a stand alone

against the stand of the whole world in matters of this kind, thongh we have had the example of New Zealand, which in 1938 did take a stand virtually alone in the world, and I believe it has earned the respect of a great number of people by reason of having taken that stand at that time. I have been completely consistent about this. I have been accused in the past of being unrealistic, idealistic, and this and that, but never before of being isolationist. I do hope therefore that this charge is disposed of now and for all time.
Just one word and then I am through. We cannot speak for the majority of people when we are speaking in this house on a matter like this, and I speak, like any other private member, only to express my own view. All we can do is to try to put forward views that will appeal as being sound views and offering the policy that should be taken. We do that with all sincerity and should do it with all frankness. But when the hon. member for York-Sunbury says he does not think that views of 'the kind I express represent the views of the majority, whereas the views he expresses are the views of the majority of Canadians, he is just matching his judgment against mine, and I think he will find that the kind of views I express, and the kind of views that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) expressed, are the views that are going to be held by an increasingly large percentage of English-speaking Canadians, just as they are by practicality all those who are not of Anglo-Saxon stock, and who represent fifty-one per cent of the people. Those views come from a consideration of what Canada's interests are. I put with my friends among the very forefront of Canada's interests, the survival of Great Britain, the strength of Great Britain and the survival of everything she stands for. It is important that we should try to understand each other. It is important to the unity of Canada that we should make an approach of that kind rather than the other approach which is what is called the British front approach. The results will be almost identical in either case; we shall work together. But it is important that we should speak as a chorus, shall I say, rather than with a single voice automatically. Because if we set out to speak with a single Voice the other nations will say, "It is just the old British voice. It is not the other democracies standing alongside her, and so they can be ignored." If we follow that course we in Canada shall have no foreign policy, and all the talk about national autonomy will -become just so much talk. We shall be setting the 
clock back and we shall not be doing the things my hon. friend wants us to do as well as if we pursued the line I suggest.
I am sorry to have taken up time with this personal explanation, but I do think it is important that in these matters on which there is so much emotional attachment we try to understand each other, and if I am not understood by my hon. friends at least I hope that they they will not doubt my loyalty on this or any other occasion.

with him and I believe the administration also is. I wish to supplement that by saying that I am not accountable for the interpretations that gentlemen opposite may put upon his words. Just before we get away from the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I want to express my personal appreciation of his having made his statement this afternoon.
I wish to make one statement regarding the reason why the British empire did1 not prevent the aggression of Japan. I have it on the very best of authority, as I believe all hon. members would recognize if I were free to divulge that authority, that the reason why Britain did not take stronger action then was that they were just too weak to do anything else. Their navy and army had fallen into disrepair, and they realized fully that if they did take a stand, the whole thing would fall on them. Following the tragic experience of Munich they simply had to begin to build up their power. Before this incident can be taken as of important historical significance one way or the other it should1 be established whether that statement which I received in confidence is true. I believe it is true, for the simple reason that I do not see how in the world the British empire could otherwise have become so impotent as it did become in just seven short years, especially when our Prime Minister himself on coming into power in 1935, immediately began to increase armaments in this country, and other empire countries were doing the same. I cannot be convinced that we had a first-class fighting force capable of meeting Japan in 1932.

If I might answer my hon. friend in a word, assuming that what he says is true, it makes even stronger than anything else could the case that I have been making-that is, that in the time that lies ahead we should endeavour to get a totality of force that will prevent aggression and prevent Great Britain or the United States from ever again being put in a position where they will have to allow an aggressor to go
ahead. Therefore I advocated in my speech, as I have done for the last ten years, that in order to prevent war and aggression you must have enough force to do it, so much force that nobody will dream of committing an act of aggression. For me it is no longer possible to find that force in any one nation. It is not possible to find it in the British commonwealth, or in Britain, the United States or in Russia, the three most powerful nations the world has ever seen. It is necessary now to find that totality of force which will prevent aggression in a combination of all the nations. I should like to see that brought about. That is what I mean when I say we must have collective action to organize collective strength. There is nothing particularly idealistic in this. It is a policy based on interest, as all policy must be based. But it is in our interests that we should work together with all nations to mobilize the greatest amount of strength we can get-if possible all strength on our side against aggression. That is fundamental in any system of security which is built up after the war. I am glad my hon. friend brought out that point; it strongly reinforces the point I was making.

In my judgment it absolutely devastates my hon. friend's contention. There must have been unquestionably a reason why the British empire allowed its fighting forces to fall into disrepair. What could that reason possibly have been? It was that the British people were lulled into a sense of security by reason of the fact that they reposed trust in the League of Nations, which was supposed to be powerful enough or diplomatic enough or wise enough to deal with all international situations as they arose. The result was that, as never before in the history of the British empire, the people allowed their defence forces to fall into disrepair. The people or the governments did that. That is a fact which in my judgment is of prime importance to this parliament to-day. There was something which caused us to allow our forces to become weak. I maintain it was the fact that we were in the League of Nations. If we can reason by reference to what has occurred in the past, if we bind ourselves into a supranational arrangement we will do exactly the same, or a little worse. We shall say it is George's business; let George do it, as we said before. George certainly left it undone. My own opinion is that George had his ear bent to the very powers that the hon. member for Macleod was referring to,

who were trying to render the British empire so weak that it was unable to stand up against its foes.
May I say something with respect to the actual power within the League of Nations. France was in the League of Nations, and there were half a dozen other nations who were members of the league. If there was any vitality or virtue in the League of Nations, or any supranational government as such, surely there were enough nations within that group to have stopped Germany at that time, to have stopped Japan -they certainly could have stopped Japan. Certainly they could have stopped Germany, because Germany had not yet begun to rearm. How these arguments can be propounded I certainly cannot understand. It must be borne in mind that the British empire did finally stand in the way of Hitler in 1939, after Germany had rearmed and while Japan was even stronger. If the British empire did stand largely alone in the path of Germany and held her, what could the British empire have done had she been prepared? The great flaw in the reasoning before the war lay in the fact that we allowed ourselves to become unprepared. I am sure hon. members must be simply nauseated when they think of our contemptible state of unpreparedness and the impotence which obtained everywhere in this country, in every branch of our defence services. The attitude of the Canadian people generally regarding matters pertaining to defence was almost as bad. The Minister of Pensions and National Health, who at that time was responsible for the department having to do with military affairs, well remembers how difficult was his task in bringing anything into this house with respect to rearmament in 1936. What was the matter? There is only one answer, so far as I can see. Those who should have been informing the Dominion of Canada on the state of unpreparedness which obtained everywhere throughout the empire, those who should have been making clear to the people of Canada that Germany was rearming, that she was becoming a terrible foe, that Japan was a terrible potential foe, that unquestionably there was danger of a clash between Japan and the United States-those men whose duty it was to be informing the people of Canada, and unquestionably the Prime Minister of Canada was one, were neglecting their task. What for? Because they wanted to win elections.

speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would tell me where he learned it.

By keeping his eyes
open and doing a little reasoning, that was all. That was all that was necessary, just keeping your eyes open and doing a little reasoning when Hitler came to power. There was no question in the wide world that he meant business, none whatever; and very soon he began to manifest signs of exceedingly dangerous strength. When he entered the Ruhr, that was a warning to everyone. Surely when he entered Austria, that was the handwriting on the wall. And the statements which he made in "Mein Kampf" show what he meant. Among other things he certainly definitely declared that France must be destroyed. The Prime Minister will remember that. I suppose they thought he was talking in his sleep when he said that, but he meant what he said, as he has clearly shown. What other warning was necessary to alarm anyone? Let me point out that the members of my party were not in a position to have access to the secret documents which should have been transmitted to the heads of the government of this country. Those documents must have been filled with causes for anxiety and fear. I was reading a book just last summer by Kurt Reiss entitled "Total Espionage," in which most damaging accusations are made with respect to Baldwin and Chamberlain, to the effect that these men were informed in detail by responsible authorities in England of the conditions which were developing in Germany, and they disregarded the warnings. If they were so warned it is hardly to be conceived that the leaders of this government were not warned. Another thing that is amazing to me and is amazing to
everyone who thinks about it in the Dominion of Canada to-day, is this: why were these warnings disregarded?
Now, with respect to the statement made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, the one thing I am worried about as a father in this country, the father of eleven children and the grandfather of five, is this:	Are these babes of mine who are
now growing up going to be victims of a betrayal similar to that in the future?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member should use a word like "betrayal". He knows as well as any other hon. member in the house that the whole feeling throughout the world for many years after the last war was that there would not be another war for a long time to come. There was a strong pacific sentiment everywhere, which those who saw the danger did their best to fight. But it was difficult to do so in those times. But do not, please, talk about people betraying others. That implies a deliberate effort on their part to deceive, and to deceive for special ends, which could not have been so with any of the men about whom the hon. member has spoken.

If my word has in any way offended the Prime Minister, then I withdraw it unqualifiedly. But I did wish to use a word strong enough to cover the situation, and I can think of nothing more effective than the word "betrayal". But may I absolve my right hon. friend from that. I will say that the information adduced in the book "Total Espionage" by Kurt Reiss is sufficient to convict the two gentlemen I have mentioned of betrayal, beyond any shadow of a doubt. They betrayed not only Great Britain, but they betrayed 650 million people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I do say the hon. member has no right to say that either of these gentlemen knowingly betrayed anyone.

I withdraw once more. But. as I said this morning, the time has come for plain speaking. And hon. members at this time must do some plain speaking, let the chips fall where they may.

Mr .BLACKMORE: I have withdrawn the word "betrayal". I am not going to give information which would tie to them the term I have used. But I could give information which could not be answered at all.
It is my anxiety that if we become involved in some supranational government, and if consequently our people become apathetic and over-confident, not only in this country but in all other countries, including the British empire and the United States, then we shall be setting the stage for a complete eclipse in the next war. And against that eventuality it becomes my duty, as a responsible member of the House of Commons in Canada, and as a voter in this country, to take precautions. I say the doctrine the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is advocating at this time in the world's history is a dangerous doctrine. Yes, it is very dangerous. Let not hon. members be deceived. There was a member, not now in the house-she was defeated in the last election-who contended with the greatest earnestness that there would never be any more war. Anyone with sense knows she was talking nonsense. But there was the danger-a lot of people believed it. They were deceived and carried away, including many hon. members in the house and many members of the Liberal party.
I am going to turn just for a moment to the question of the prevalence of the belief that there would be no future war. Probably I should not go into detail, but judging from evidence brought to my attention when I was teaching school some years ago, I am convinced that an attitude of mind was deliberately induced by making use of a clever type of propaganda operating through certain (periodicals in this country, and gaining access to the teachers in our schools. The people who issued that propaganda achieved their ends, just as they intended to do. I would rather not name the people involved, but I will tell the committee this, that they were seeking deliberately to destroy the British empire. I read one of their documents which came to my hand as principal of Raymond high school. In that document they outlined their plan, and the first thing they were going to do was to destroy the fighting morale of the British people, the Anglo-Saxon race. They surely did that; they had wonderful success. Then they reasoned that when fighting morale was 
destroyed the people would oppose preparation for war-which they did. This would leave the people completely helpless at some future time, if a war were developed.
The whole thing worked out. Can we give any reason why the Anglo-Saxon world went -well, there is only one word which seems to fit, and that is, haywire? My right hon. friend knows the difficulty Mr. Roosevelt had to get the people in the United States to look upon the situation with even a measure of common sense, factuality and reality. Why, one man down there-I have forgotten his name-said, "I would not go to the Georgia river to meet the foe!" What an inconceivable dolt, to make a remark like that! And he left his country so helpless that it finally became necessary for him, and it will probably be necessary for his descendants, to go much farther than the Georgia river to meet the foe. If he had used anything like common sense, he, his sons and his fellow countrymen would have been prepared, instead of being in the pitiful state of unpreparedness in which they were, when war finally came to them.
I apologize again for occupying so much of the time of the committee, but-
The hon. member has spoken forty minutes.
I am surprised. I have found it a very interesting subject. But, Mr. Chairman, I am going to repeat this warning, time and again, so that all will come to know it.

Mr. Chairman, this discussion has amazed me. I was not a member of the house during the time mentioned by the hon. member for Lethbridge. In those days I was just an ordinary day worker. But I did pay some attention to the matters which have been discussed this afternoon. I have been amazed at the lack of knowledge shown by the men who represented the people in those days.
Summing up the war situation this morning, the Prime Minister pointed out the seriousness of the present situation, brought about by the fact that Canadian troops are actually engaged in combat. In his statement he said he wished to guarantee the troops and the general public that so far as the Canadian government was concerned, those troops would not be let down. I hope the government'will live up to that promise.
There has been some discussion this afternoon respecting the League of Nations, its break-down, and the fact that in 1939 we were plunged into a bigger and better war.

War Appropriation-External Affairs
The point which stands out clearly from the discussion is that guarantees given in all sincerity, as was the one this morning by the Prime Minister, were not lived up to. It was not the machinery of the League of Nations that failed. The machinery of the league in my opinion was a hundred per cent correct. It was the only machinery befitting this day and age. Sensible men and women sat around the conference table, arbitrating the grievances of nations, and made decisions without resort to war. Those who conceived the idea of the league were honest, and it was their belief that those who would administer the league's policy would give honest administration. Those who were administering the machinery could have made it work, but they were thinking in terms of dollars and cents rather than human needs and1 civilization. They are the ones who are responsible for the condition the world is in to-day. That is the one thing that Stands out most clearly in this discussion so far as I am concerned. Promises, such as those made by the Prime Minister this morning, were not lived up to. The men who fought accepted the promises made in 1914-18; they believed that they were fighting a war that was to end all war. The people by and large were convinced that they had accomplished, that purpose. The soldiers who had fought believed that that purpose had been accomplished. The people who are indicted by the discussion this afternoon are those who were in authority at that time, those who made the promises, those who had the administration of the world under their hands for the following twenty-five years. They fell down on the job and brought about the results we are faced with to-day.
I hope that the lesson is one that will sink into the minds of the Canadian people and the peoples of the world in general. I hope they will not place too much trust in the promises of individuals or scraps of paper such as treaties and. so forth. They themselves must take an active interest in the affairs of their country and of the world in general. They must see to it that the power to bring about a similar situation in the next generation is not left in the hands of a few men who are to make the decisions.
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has left the chamber, but I want .to say to him that I have followed very closely the workings of the League of Nations. I did a lot of work for it in my own province, because I believed in it. I also believed that we had fought a war to end war. We all know what happened to the League of Nations.
The United States, which gave birth to the idea, never became a member. That hurt the league, and hurt it badly. We all watched the manipulations from the inside. I merely have to draw your attention to the men in France and England who were responsible for the break-down of the league. These countries were the dominant factors in the league and1 they could have made it work. Those most prominent in bringing about the downfall of the League of Nations were Sir Samuel Hoare and Mr. Pierre Laval. They stood by and allowed Mussolini to carry on his adventure in Ethiopia. We know to-day the motives that actuated them. We know where Hoare is to-day. He is in Spain with Franco, because he is acceptable to Franco. We know where Laval is to-day.
I have no intention of going into this particular matter. It is a long story and I think everybody is familiar with it. I do not think the ideas advanced by the hon. member for Lethbridge are relevant at all. I do not believe in imposing some superstructure on the world as an aftermath of this war. We must have an organization similar to the League of Nations as a means of ironing out our difficulties. But you must have honest men and women in this organization who will stand up and fight for the proper principles. That was not done in the last war. I can remember the discussions that took place on the Versailles treaty. Some of us who were fairly young at that time knew that we were merely laying the basis for another war. The job should have been completed. Foch should have been listened to. He warned the people who were signing the Versailles treaty that they were merely signing an armistice and making it necessary to do the job over again within twenty-five years. He was ready and willing to complete the job, and it should have been completed. But the soldiers won the war and the politicians stole the peace. They manipulated things and brought about the situation we are in to-day.
When the peace is being written this time, many of the men who are actually in the field and have experienced the horrors of war should be given the privilege of sitting around the conference table and having something to say about the machinery that will be provided as an aftermath of this war. I did not get up to say these things, but the discussion which took place previously provoked me into saying what I have said. I could not help making these remarks with respect to the League of Nations. I never had any doubt as to whether it was the right

machinery. If it had been, made to work, we would not be at war to-day. I know why we are at war to-day. Canada was blindly led by people in whom she had confidence. It has always been my opinion that Canada blindly followed Great Britain's lead and we eventually landed in the position we are in to-day. They will be indicted for creating the situation in which we find ourselves to-day.
If Churchill had had anything to say about what was done in Great Britain in the ten years before the war, we would not be in the situation we are in to-day. He tried constantly to warn them of what was taking place. We all know why the strength of Hitler was built up. There is no mystery about it. We know why British and French money was provided. They feared social change more than they feared Hitler. They feared Russia as being the vanguard of social change. They wanted a strong Hitler in Europe to offset any efforts to bring about social change. That is why the machinery to avoid war in the future broke down. I think it is the duty of the government and of those who represent the people, of those who have access to this information, to bring these facts before the public from time to time so that there may not be repetition in the future of what we are going through to-day.
I do not think the time is opportune to discuss foreign policy. The policy of the government to-day should be to make every effort to win the war. The discussion of just how we are going to do business with our neighbours in the future should be left until the picture is clearer than it is at the present time, until we know just what kind of world we are going to be living in.
I should like to say a few words about a matter in connection with which I think Canada should do something at this time. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) raised a question on Friday evening which seemed to not be very popular. He asked that some assistance be given to the Jewish people. This is a matter about which the government should make some pronouncement. To hear some people talk you would think the Jews represented seventy-five per cent of the world's population, when the fact is that there are probably less than 10,000,000 Jews in the world. About 7,500,000 of these are in nazi-occupied Europe. I do not want to elaborate on some of the things said by the hon. member, but we must not

forget that Hitler has a policy of complete extermination of these people before the end of the year. I am not interested in them as a race, but we are all human, and I try to place myself in the position of one of these people who are in nazi-occupied Europe. They go through the same suffering that you would if you were starving or waiting for a firing squad, if you were placed in a box-car and shipped away among the dead, if you were faced by all the horrors described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. If there is something we can do about it, we should do it. I am very critical of everything that has been done so far. The Bermuda conference which was called to discuss the question of refugees from occupied countries did absolutely nothing about the question. I have read a little about the conference. Delegates of the different countries came there with fixed policies from their governments, and it was merely a matter of doing nothing. There is no policy to-day on that question. One thing which Canada could do is to make representations to the British government. There is available in Palestine a ready and convenient sanctuary for a considerable number of Jews. Palestine is an example of 1914-18 promises which were not lived up to by the British government. Everybody in this house knows about the Balfour declaration issued on December 2, 1917, whereby Palestine was to be made a homeland for the Jewish people. They were to be given their roots in the soil of some country so that they could take on the status of a nation and be represented in the future world on that basis. That declaration has been partly put into effect, but what concerns me is that, according to a white paper issued by the British colonial office within the last six weeks, Jewish immigration to Palestine for this year is cut down to a greater extent than it has been in the past, and for next year, 1944, it is eliminated completely.
The Jews as a people are making a contribution in this war. They are serving in the allied armies at the present time in North Africa and wherever the war is being carried on. Some 30,000 Jewish soldiers are fighting in the allied forces. In relation to the number of Jewish people throughout the world and their meagre opportunities of participation, they are making their contribution, and there is no reason in the world why the Balfour declaration should not be carried out. Remember that it was backed up by the United States. I have here a declaration passed by the 77th congress, bearing the signatures of practically all the United States senators and members of the House

War Appropriation-External Affairs
of Representatives, entitled "A common purpose of civilized mankind". It deals specifically with the question of Palestine. I am not concerned about Palestine as a homeland of the Jewish people; that is something which will have to be decided by themselves and the British government. What I am concerned about is that Palestine offers a sanctuary for thousands of Jewish people who might make their way out of nazi-occupied Europe if they had anywhere to go. The action of the British government has closed to them a door which was opened by their own people. They are not able to go there.
I cannot understand how any member of a government or any member of parliament can stand up and make the declarations that are made about serving humanity, about the better world which is to come when all this destruction and misery have ceased, and yet preclude the possibility of enabling the Jewish people who are being persecuted in nazi-occupied Europe to pass through the door , which their friends in Palestine have opened to them. Canada has said nothing on this matter, and she has the right to say something. I feel we have the right to protest this action on the part of the British government. They have no right to close that door to Palestine when the Jewish people are willing to open it and to accept full responsibility now and in the future for those who may be able to escape from nazi-occupied Europe.
In the next place, entrance to neutral countries to which these people might be able to escape is practically closed. The great democracies who are engaged in the war have undetraken to liberate all the peoples of Europe some time in the future, but neither they nor ourselves have ever said that they were prepared to help to pay the bill of refugees who might be able to escape to those neutral countries. The action of the united nations regarding the Jewish people can only be described as hypocritical. I do not know how any man or any woman can presume to stand up in this chamber and make promises to those who may happen to come through this war, while they will not lift a finger to provide a sanctuary for thousands of people who could probably get away from nazi-occupied countries if they could be maintained in Switzerland and other neutral states. We should be prepared to bear our proportion of the cost of maintenance of these people and some reasonable disposition to provide for their welfare after the war. It is not a matter of leaving the neutral countries to handle the job alone.
The other evening, when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was speaking on this question, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) got up and tried to give it a political significance. So far as I am concerned the human race is one family. Where you were born, what is your religion, or your nationality, or the colour of your skin, is an accident of birth; you are not responsible for it. Unless we break down this idea of merely regarding as Canadians those who were born in Canada, I can see very little hope for the future of the world on the basis of the promises which are now being made concerning post-war policies. I think we could start doing something now. I have many documents here. I am not going to read them; I do not believe in quoting too much, but they contain the assurance by people who know what they are talking about that if the doors into Palestine were opened, thousands of Jewish people could make their way there and find a sanctuary.
To my mind the handling of this question by the united nations as a whole will stand out as one of the strongest indictments against us. We have not lifted a finger to save thousands and thousands of lives. We say that when the war is over Hitler will be brought to task and made to pay for his atrocities against the persecuted peoples of Europe. That is all very well as regards the nations who are recognized as such, who will have their representatives at the conference table to present their case for them. But that is not the position of the Jews, and no other class of people in Europe have suffered such severe persecution. Where Hitler has been able to enter and dominate they have lost all their worldy goods; their families have been destroyed or scattered, and they have suffered most inhuman treatment. But they will not be sitting around the conference table; and if the attitude of the united nations now towards rescuing them while there is still a chance of rescue is to dominate at the conference table, we do not mean anything when we say that the atrocities for which the Germans and the Italians are responsible will have to be paid for. We can do something about it. But we have never even lifted a finger.

My hon. friend says we have not lifted a finger. Does he attach no importance whatever to all the Canadian army, navy and air forces are dloing in this war to try to alleviate the situation in Europe, and in particular, the terrible position of those very people of whom he is speaking? How can he say that this country has not
