War Appropriation-External Affairs
lifted a finger? I made very clear in the statement I put forward the other day that the difficulty of obtaining passage on ships to bring people to this side was one of the reasons why some of the refugees who have escaped could not be brought here, but I have made it equally clear that where it was possible to have them brought over, Canada was )repared to receive them.

The Prime Minister and myself are talking about two different things. [ am referring now particularly to the possibilities of saving thousands and thousands of Jewish lives in nazi-occupied Europe. I recognize what we are doing to liberate the whole continent of Europe, but the Jewish people face a different situation altogether. We may be able to liberate to some extent the French and the Belgians. They will be able to take part in the fight. But the Jewish people have been driven into Poland, largely into ghettos, without any chance to fight for themselves, and if our attitude prevails they will not be there when the liberation takes place, because they are being systematically exterminated day by day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How can we possibly get into Germany to liberate them or to prevent them from being put into ghettos? The one hope for them is that our military action along with that of other allied nations may help to make possible their speedy release, but until that time comes what can we do for persons who are now in Germany or enemy occupied countries?

I am not asking the government to get into Europe in order to do this. I am asking the Canadian government to protest to the British government against their action in closing the doors of Palestine to Jewish refugees who may escape from nazi-occupied Europe. I said that I would ask the government to do only some of the things I think we can do, and I suggest that we can make that protest. If thousands of refugees vdio are escaping had the right to go into Palestine, they could be taken care of in that way. The action of the British government in closing that door, restricting immigration this year to 29,000 and next year completely cutting it off, is something we can protest against.
How long ago was it that the British government made that decision to close Palestine?

Within the last six weeks.
It is a white paper issued by the colonial office. That is one thing I should like to see done. Second, I think the neutral countries that are

closed would get thousands of these people if those countries had some assurance that the United States or Canada or some other country could be provided as a sanctuary for them if they could be transported or that we would assist neutral countries in helping to feed them. I cannot forget the fact the Prime Minister mentions ships and railways and all these difficulties. All I ask is that the Canadian government indicate what they are prepared to do by way of helping these people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that I made a definite statement in that regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Read page 4560 of Hansard.

A large number of Jewish
people did get hold of a ship themselves last year and sailed with hundreds of women and children from port to port, but they were refused entry until the ship finally broke up off the coast of Norway somewhere. What I have suggested are things that we can do. Canada has a right to speak in these matters and to protest against the closing of Palestine, not taking sides as to whether Zionism is right or wrong; but I submit that that door should be opened and as many people allowed in as possible if they can escape. They are penned in and have nowhere to go. We could say that we are willing to take them, provided they can get here; that we would see that they were looked after and that some final disposition could be made after the war of the question of their home status.

What was the reason
given by the British government for closing Palestine? I am only seeking information to enlighten myself on that point.

No reason has been given
that I know of, apart from the fact that they have a mandate over Palestine and have the right to decide about immigration. My opinion is that it is a case of the old appeasement policy, appeasing the Arabs, and failing to face a realistic situation on a humanitarian basis.

Was it debated in the
British House of Commons?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I point
out to the hon. member that the immigration policy is still governed by the terms of the white paper which was issued in 1939. The recent statement of policy referred to was an

War Appropriation-External Affairs
announcement some weeks ago that the 1935 white paper policy remained in force and would not be reopened at this moment.

That is true, but that 1939 paper definitely sets out that at the end of 1943 there shall be no more immigration into Palestine, and immigration, is badly restricted this year. It reiterates the previous policy and closes the door at the end of 1944.
This is not a new policy to which the hon. member has referred-the announcement of six weeks ago?

It was a paper that was
issued reiterating the previous policy on account of representations made to open the door. Their answer was a reiteration of that previous policy which closes it in 1944.
There has not been any change in policy. This is a confirmation of an old policy?
Not since 1939.

The only thing I am
concerned about is that it did seem to me that in the last day or so the Jewish people have had a lot of champions. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the committee.
I will give the hon. member a file that goes back to 1939. It is not to-day that I beoame interested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To supplement what I have said to my hon. friend, the 1939 document laid down an annual immigration quota for each year up to 1944 and the United Kingdom is advancing some visas, normally valid in 1944, to help some of these refugees this year.

As the Prime Minister knows, the people of British Columbia are keenly interested in the government's foreign policy, particularly in so far as it refers to the Japanese evacuees. In fact, the feeling has been so tense that it was made clear to the government that it may anticipate trouble should there be any attempt at the end of the war to return the evacuees to the Pacific coast. However, the door has been closed, partly at any rate, in this direction by reason of the fact that the custodian of enemy property has sold to the veterans' land board some 760 odd parcels of agricultural land formerly occupied by Japanese, so that the question arises, where does the government intend to place the evacuees at the close of the war? In my district of Kootenay West there are 8,000 of them, and their attitude is apparently tranquil
enough at present. But the time will come when the attention of the allies is directed exclusively to Japan, and it may be that the spirit of loyalty may prompt these evacuees to change their attitude, which would be particularly dangerous if directed to the railroads and power plants, because many of them are in that vicinity. I would ask the Prime Minister, before . these estimates are passed, to tell us just what the government's foreign policy is toward these evacuees; for instance, what it is towards the 10,000 nationals? Is it the intention to return them to Japan or to have them remain in Canada? What would be the government's policy toward the 7,000 naturalized Japanese and toward the 6,000 Canadian-born Japanese? As to these naturalized Japanese, of course that is optional with the government, because they can cancel naturalization if the situation warrants it. As to the Canadian-born Japanese it seems to me that their citizenship should be respected. That is the question I should like the Prime Minister to make clear before we pass upon these estimates. We are keenly interested in knowing whether we are to have eight thousand Japanese permanently located in the interior of British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of entering into a discussion of Canada's general foreign policy. I wish to confine my remarks to one particular phase of that policy and to something which I think Canada can do, and certainly it is a phase of our foreign policy to which Canada should give some consideration at the present time.
As one who has spent just about half his lifetime in Canada and the other half in that small sister dominion which has recently given up its dominion status, the little island of Newfoundland, I am anxious to know what consideration is being given at the present time to the relationship that is to exist between Canada and Newfoundland when the war ends. This is opportune to the subject of discussion at the present time and one of considerable importance to Canada.
If hon. members will for a moment visualize the geographical position and the strategic position which Newfoundland holds in the lower St. Lawrence, I think they will fully realize the importance of that island to Canada. We have only to think for a moment of how difficult it would be to defend Canada and this continent if to-day an enemy were in possession of that island. Situated as she is in the mouth of the St. Lawrence, the country that dominates Newfoundland is in a position to sail up the St. Lawrence and
4658	COMMONS
War Appropriation-External Affairs
destroy Canada's lifeline of trade with Britain and Europe. There is an importance there that has not been recognized in the past.
We have been content to depend for our security upon the British navy, and upon the Monroe doctrine to a considerable extent, until this war came. But now that Canada considers herself a nation and is certainly in a position where she must assume some responsibility for her own defence in the future, and with the growing importance of submarines and air power, the strategic position of that island becomes important for Canada's defence. That importance is recognized, as every hon. member knows, by Great Britain and by the United States of America as well as by Canada. To-day it forms a vital line in North America's defence. There has taken place the peaceful invasion of the island by Canadian, American and British members of the armed forces. A writer in the Yale Review for the spring of 1943 likens the island at present to a huge anchored aircraft carrier, combined with a great natural dry dock moored to the ocean floor. That importance I need not emphasize or dwell upon.
History before now has demonstrated the strategic importance of Newfoundland to the country that held it. I think historians are agreed that probably one of the mistakes that the French rhade when they sought to maintain occupation of this continent was that in their interest in the fur trade they failed completely to recognize the importance of that island set squarely across the entrance to the St. Lawrence. It was not until 1662 that the French realized it would be important to them in holding Canada and North America to secure possession of that island. By that time it was too late. Great Britain had established her power on that island. Historians agree that when the French lost possession of the peninsula of Avalon that was the first step in the downfall of the French power on this continent. England's possession of that little island gave her the use of its harbours and a decided advantage over the French in the wars that followed between England and France. I need not emphasize the importance of that island to Great Britain at the time of the American revolution and the American invasion of Canada. The fact that that island was then a British possession, that British ships crossing the Atlantic could find shelter there and from there proceed up the St. Lawrence to the relief of those who were holding Quebec was a vital factor in the results that followed that invasion.
I should like for a moment to call the attention of the committee to the fact that in 1776, when Quebec was the last fortified position in British possession, when the garrison

at Quebec numbered very little more than one hundred men, the presence of two schooner-loads of soldiers from Newfoundland, to the number of, I believe, 130, has generally been recognized to have been of considerable help to that little garrison on that night of January 1, 1776. I am glad to know that years later, in 1846, when the one city in that island. St. John's, was half destroyed by fire, Canada was the first to come to the assistance of its people. I well remember as a boy in the public schools many years after that learning of the gratitude of the people of Newfoundland for the assistance which had come first of all from Canada on that occasion when Newfoundland needed help. The point I wish to call to the attention of the committee is that history has shown in the past that the country which held this part of North America found it extremely important to be in possession of that outpost of the St. Jjawrence, that little island which is known to-day as the watchdog of the St. Lawrence.
I am anxious to learn from the Prime Minister whether any consideration is being given at the present time to the question of the union of that island with the Dominion of Canada. I am satisfied that the future fortune of that island lies in common with Canada's future. I am anxious to see steps initiated by the Canadian government with that end in view. I have said that the time is now opportune. Hon. members will recall that back in 1933 when that little island found more than one-third of its revenue going to the payment of externally held debts they realized it was utterly impossible, on account of the loss of their markets for fish, to carry on, and they voluntarily relinquished responsible government which they had enjoyed for nearly one hundred years. I believe they are the only example of any part of the British empire, which possessed dominion status under the statute of Westminster, voluntarily relinquishing that dominion status. They were forced to do so by economic pressure. To-day there is a growing discontent with the government by commission. There are strong interests in the island at work looking toward the restoration of responsible government when the war ends. So far as the status of the island is concerned, some change will undoubtedly have to be faced. That in itself offers an opportunity for reopening the old question of union with the Dominion of Canada. There has grown up in the island during the past two or three years, as a result of the seeds of social changes which have been planted there by the presence of Canadian and American members of the armed forces, a feeling that the economic well-being and the strategic needs

War Appropriation-External Affairs
of that island require some kind of union with either Canada or the United States. As I say, that feeling has grown.
From all the information I can gather I believe the people of Newfoundland have come to recognize the fact that their future economic well-being lies along the road of some form of union with either Canada or the United States. Their history, first as an isolated colony and then as an isolated dominion, has been a very unhappy one. There are probably few parts of the civilized world to-day where the common people have suffered as much from exploitation as the inhabitants of Newfoundland have suffered during the periods that have passed. There are many who know the island well who fear for some reason the importance of United States influence there at the present time. The inpouring of United States dollars which has taken place during the war, the first-hand observation of United States standards of living, are all having a significant appeal to the people of that island, the people who lived through a depression when 25 per cent of the population was living on a dole of 6 cents a day. One cannot wonder that the presence of United States money and the knowledge of United States standards of living are making a significant appeal to some of the people.
There are also factors growing out of the past which give the people of that little island some reason to be a little suspicious of union with Canada, and I am confident that such a union as I have suggested will not be achieved without difficulty. It will require far-sighted statesmanship to bring about such an objective; it will require statesmen who are fully appreciative of the importance to Canada of this union, important from the point of view of the defence of this country in the future. It will depend upon the readiness of these statesmen to accord generous terms to the people of that island in order to effect such a union.
May I inquire from the hon. member the population of Newfoundland?
The population at the present time is somewhere around three hundred thousand.
Homogeneous population?

I would say that the inhabitants of the island are all of British descent. There has been no immigration from Europe. Up until twenty-five years ago the memory of what happened in 1895 when representatives from Newfoundland, anxious to bring about union, failed in their negotiations and when I think the whole question turned on the
payment of somewhere around one million dollars by the Canadian parliament, has caused considerable opposition to union with Canada. That has been developed in the country over the years; but there are many factors that will facilitate the work of any Canadian government that will to-day undertake negotiations with that end in view. In the first place we can rely on the loyalty of the people of that island to Great Britain. I need not emphasize that loyalty; I think it has been demonstrated in every war in which England has been engaged within recent times.
The Canadian government took what is generally considered a commendable step in their appointment of the present high commissioner to Newfoundland, Mr. Charles J. Burchell. The people from the island to whom I have spoken use the highest terms of commendation in referring to the good work he has done. The fact that the people there can deal with the Canadian government through a high commissioner instead of dealing through a branch of the colonial office, as the United States government has required them to do, has raised the prestige of the Canadian government in the minds of those people, and will assist greatly in any negotiations that may be undertaken.
May I close with an appeal to the government that they recognize the importance of that union to Canada. I am not thinking so much of the interests of Newfoundland itself. Having lived in both parts of the empire, and knowing both parts well, I am satisfied that the future success of that island lies in a union with Canada. I am satisfied that Newfoundland needs Canada, and also that Canada needs Newfoundland. I should like to emphasize the importance of beginning negotiations at once because, as soon as the war ends, questions connected with the withdrawal of Canadian airmen, soldiers and members of the Canadian navy, and the withdrawal of United States members of the armed forces, as well as the question as to the disposition to be made of the bases established by both Canadian and United States governments, will be matters which will have to be determined. I would suggest that steps be initiated now toward sounding out the possibility of making Newfoundland the youngest province of Canada, after the war, and the rounding out of the Dominion of Canada by the union of that island with us.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to add a few remarks to those I made last Friday evening, but before I do so may I pay tribute to the Prime Minis-
4660	COMMONS
War Appropriation-External Affairs
ter (Mr. Mackenzie King). I should like to call the attention of people outside the house, who perhaps do not realize what he is doing, that to sit as he did last Friday-not only to sit, but to listen and, I have no doubt, pay attention-through nine hours of debate in weather such as this is, to say the least, no mean feat of endurance. I do not know how he feels to-day, but I can say that I have often felt a lot more like speaking than I do now.
And we have to keep our coats on, too.

Well, as long as we keep our shirts on, we shall be all right. So that I am sure hon. members will overlook any shortcomings in my manner of speaking.
All hon. members listened this morning with feelings of gratitude and thankfulness to the great news from Europe. I know no remarks 'of mine can add to what was said in the house. I do not feel, however, that happenings in Europe should cause any diminution in our efforts to do the best we can in the House of Commons on behalf of those who are doing the fighting. The allied nations are subjecting the gangsters to a continual bombardment of two-ton and four-ton blockbusters, and meanwhile the racketeers seem to be subjecting the allies to a continuous bombardment of two-ton truth-busters.
May I call the attention of the committee to a letter published in the New York Times on May 9. It is headed "A Mission To Moscow", and the authors are John Dewey and Suzanne LaFollette who, respectively, were chairman and secretary of the international mission of inquiry into the Moscow trials. I shall not read the whole letter, on account of its length; I shall read the first and last paragraphs. It begins:
The film "Mission to Moscow" is the first instance in our country of totalitarian propa-ganada for mass consumption-a propaganda which falsifies history through distortion, omission or pure invention of facts, and whose effect can only he to confuse the public in its thought and its loyalties.
Even in a fictional film this method would be disturbing. It becomes alarming in a film presented as factual and documentary, and introducing living historical personalities. Our former ambassador to the Soviet Union, Joseph E. Davies, personally introduces this dramatization of his mission as the "truth" about Russia. And the representation of President Roosevelt talking to Mr. Davies of the film seems to suggest that it is at least semi-official.
That was the first paragraph. This is the last one:
The film is anti-British, anti-congress, antidemocratic and anti-truth. It deepens that crisis in morals which is the fundamental issue in the modern world. . . . "Mission to Moscow"

is a major defeat for the democratic cause. In putting out this picture the producers, far from rendering the patriotic service on which Mr. Davies compliments them, have assailed the very foundations of freedom. For truth and freedom are indivisible, as Hitler knew when he expounded his method of confusing public opinion through propaganda. The picture "Mission to Moscow" makes skilful use of the Hitler technique. To quote Matthew Low of the New Leader: "This kind of 'truth' is on the march, and God help us if nothing can stop it."
I do not wish to add any remarks. I did not see the film, and I do not intend to see it. But I ask this: How is it proposed to build the four freedoms on a foundation of falsehoods, when truth and liberty are indivisible? I think that is a fair question, but I shall leave others to answer it. It is written, as near as I can remember, "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." Or, as I have just said, truth and freedom are indivisible. I would advise the examination by everybody of all propaganda, of all proposals for a new order, for a new world, if you like, from that point of view. Let everyone ask himself two questions. Is it the truth? If it is not, then it will make to destroy liberty. Does it propose to curtail liberty? If so, it is not the truth.
Some months ago I raised a question in this house in connection with our loyalty to the crown. This matter had been brought up in a speech by Mr. Sandwell who advised that the people of Canada would have to surrender their loyalty to the crown as individuals to an international control.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: He never suggested that at all.
He said that we might perhaps have to surrender some part of our sovereignty.

It would mean a diminution of our liberty as individuals, but I am not going to argue the point to-day. The press were flattering to me and to my colleague here. I should like to quote an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, as follows:
There should be no mystery about where Mr. Jaques got his ideas. He is a student of Major C. H. Douglas, the originator of Social Credit theory, and Major Douglas provided the lead his students and followers require in Jew-baiting. Major Douglas wrote his main work "Social Credit" in 1924, about the same time as Adolf Hitler was completing "Mein Kampf", and by curious coincidence, both these works bore the influence of an earlier work called "The Protocols of the Learned Elders of Zion."

War Appropriation-External Affairs
That is a very good illustration of what I have said, that truth and liberty are indivisible. But to say that Major Douglas based his ideas upon those of Adolf Hitler is about as damnable a lie as it is possible to utter. Certainly it is a credit to the opposition of social credit. Major Douglas introduced his idea in New York, either late ini 1918 or early in 1919, while Adolf Hitler was still a corporal in the imperial German army. I do not suppose "Mein Kampf", or the ideas expressed therein, had entered his head, but anything to destroy truth, and see if you can link up anti-semitism and fascism to social credit. Personally I do not care. It will not make any difference to me, but I warn the people to make sure whether these statements are true or false. If they are false, you can be sure that there is a purpose behind them.
I have been told by numerous people and it has been stated in the press that I had perpetrated the greatest waste of parliamentary time in parliamentary history. This was said merely because I had called the attention of the people to the fact that there is a movement which would surrender our loyalty to the crown, which is the symbol of our individual liberties, to international control. The editor of Saturday Night honoured me with a complete editorial about myself and this supposed waste of time, and then he devoted two pages to the idea. I notice the same thing in other papers of Canada. He was good enough to end up by saying:
Mr. Jaques further distinguished himself a few days later by upholding, in (of all places) Miss Judith Robinson's News, the authenticity of the "Protocols of the Elders of Zion," that astounding fabrication which purports to record the proceedings of a conference of highly placed Jews held for the purpose of planning the destruction of Christian civilization. Presumably a mentality which can accept the A plus B theorem can accept anything.
That is very touching. The A plus B theorem I need hardly explain is the proof that there is a shortage of purchasing power. Evidently the editor of Saturday Night, Mr. Sandwell, does not believe in it, or at least he does not believe in it by inference. But unless he is stupid beyond belief he must believe in it. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this would seem to be a convenient opportunity to make a general statement on our relations with our neighbours in the Latin American countries.
There has been a natural and very marked growth of interest recently in our contacts with Latin America. Our newspapers, magazines and radio programmes all bear witness to this growth. So also does the increased enrolment in college classes in Spanish and Portuguese. Inquiries from commercial organizations and questions asked in this house reflect the same interest, and I shall be glad on this occasion to add a little to the information which has from time to time been given to the house.
May I say at the outset that it is gratifying to note that the growth of Canadian interest in the countries of Latin America is matched by a parallel development of interest in Canada on the part of our friends from south of the Rio Grande. We have been happy to welcome in recent months the foreign minister of

War Appropriation-External Affairs
Uruguay, the president of Bolivia, the former president of Colombia and a number of other distinguished visitors from Latin America. We were looking forward to a visit from the president of Chile which unfortunately has had to be postponed. In addition, Canada has welcomed groups of journalists from Argentina, Chile, Paraguay, Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Mexico, Bolivia and Cuba.
This growth of mutual interest is undoubtedly due in considerable measure to the fact that, with one exception, which *we all hope will not long remain an exception, the nations of North and South America have come to a clear and formal recognition of the common danger in which we stand. The democratic and Christian ideals in which we have all been nurtured are menaced by enemies more dangerous than any aggressor in the history of western civilization. Under such circumstances it is right and natural that we should draw closer to those who are our friends and, in particular, to those who fight with us. But in addition to this immediate cause for the establishment of closer relations with our Latin American neighbours there is a growing realization that in the post-war era, as well as in the period of conflict, we shall have interests in common; that our joint contributions to the peace and welfare of the wTorld as a whole can and must be based on a joint and effective interest in the welfare and peace of our own neighbourhood. It is thus a matter of significance, and a sound cause for satisfaction, that we have constantly increasing evidence of the growth of mutual knowledge, mutual respect and mutual good>-will among the nations of this hemisphere.
It would perhaps be useful at this point to place on Hansard a factual record of the official contacts maintained by Canada in the Latin American countries. As hon. members are aware, we have established legations in Argentina, Brazil and Chile. In each of these countries the officer of the commercial intel-ligerfce service who previously acted as trade commissioner is now a member of the staff of the legation with the title of commercial attache. The legations are under the supervision of the Department of External Affairs and report to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Under the Department of Trade and Commerce the commercial intelligence service maintains trade commissioners in Cuba, Mexico, Panama-shortly to be moved to Colombia -and Peru. The responsibilities of the commercial attaches and trade commissioners in certain cases extend beyond the boundaries of 72537-2954
the country in which they reside with the result that every country in Latin America is within the field of activity of a trade representative of the Canadian government.
Our official contacts with the governments I have mentioned have been reciprocated by the establishment of legations in Ottawa by the governments of Argentina, Brazil and Chile. In addition, there are in Canada consular representatives of Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, Haiti, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Salvador, and Venezuela. Canada has no consulates in Latin America, our only offices of this kind at present being the newly-established consulate general in New York and consulates in St. Pierre and Miquelon, and Greenland. Consideration is being given to the establishment of additional consular offices but no decision has yet been taken.
Our legations in Brazil and Argentina were established in 1941. Our first minister accredited only to Chile was appointed in 1942. The government has been repeatedly urged by representatives of business organizations and others to extend our diplomatic representation in Latin America and we have received proposals looking towards the exchange of ministers from a number of other Latin American governments.
Much as we should like to accede to these proposals, we have found it necessary to move slowly. The major difficulty has been the problem of personnel. It is an ironic fact that the very time when it is particularly important that we should be well and widely represented in friendly foreign countries is the time when the pressure on Canadian man-power is greatest and when it is most difficult to spare from urgent forms of national service persons suitable for appointment to tne posts of minister and to the subordinate offices in the proposed legations. It is almost impossible at present to provide any more of the senior officers of the permanent external service for appointment as ministers abroad. We have already reduced our establishment of trained senior personnel in Ottawa and in our present legations and high commissioners' offices to the point where those who are left are carrying a burden sc* heavy that we cannot add to it by further withdrawals without creating more problems; than we solve. Most of those outside the service with the kind of qualifications required by persons apointed to diplomatic posts are already so deeply engaged in activities in close connection with the national war effort, that they cannot justly be urged to undertake appointments abroad. Nothing would be more unsatisfactory or more likely to arouse just

War Appiupriation-External Affairs
and severe condemnation among our people at home than to send incompetent or unsuitable persons as the diplomatic representatives of Canada in foreign countries.
The same problem exists in great measure with respect to the secretarial posts in our legations. The Department of External Affairs grew slowly for many years and the necessity for economy during the thirties precluded the enlistment and training of as many young men as should otherwise have been enrolled. Now that the necessity of expansion has arisen we find that even by spreading our trained officers very thinly over the field, we cannot cover all the ground that should be occupied. Here again the problems of recruitment have been seriously complicated at the very time when good candidates for the service are most required. A very large proportion of the best young manhood of this country is in the armed forces and selective service rules made it almost impossible -and I do not criticize the regulations-to accept applications from others who are physically fit. Moreover, if we were to fill the service now with young men who had not enlisted to fight for their country those who have joined the army or navy or air force would find their entrance to and advancement in the external service blocked or impeded by the appointments made during their absence on active service. This would be manifestly unfair.
Faced with this problem the civil service commission has held only one examination for appointments to the post of third secretary in the Department of External Affairs in the last three years. That examination, held in 1941, was arranged particularly to fill the definite need arising from our increased contacts with Latin America. It was specifically designed for candidates with a knowledge of Spanish or Portuguese. There were 134 applicants for permission to write, thirty actually wrote and of these five qualified and were appointed to the external affairs service.
Apart from this small group, appointments to the service have been temporary war-time assignments. But even if we could get enough candidates and of the right quality for such appointments, it takes time to train the new officers and to enable them to obtain the experience that is so necessary for those who serve abroad.
These are some of the difficulties with which the service is faced and I admit that I do not see any easy or wholly satisfactory solution to it. It is a simple statement of fact that in external affairs, as in certain other

branches of government, in business and in some professions, there are not now available in Canada enough men of the required training and experience to fill the posts that should be filled.
Nevertheless and in spite of the difficulties which I have described it has now become apparent that we cannot much longer delay a further extension of our diplomatic representation in Latin America. Mexico is a case particularly in point. I do not think we should longer delay the establishment of a legation in Mexico City, and I hope that provision for such an office will be included in supplementary estimates to be brought down later in the session. Similarly I hope to be able to announce an agreement to open legations in Cuba and Peru. In some way the difficulty of finding personnel will have to be overcome.
Before concluding my discussion of this problem, may I suggest that hon. members who are interested in the problems to which I have briefly referred may find it interesting and useful to examine the recent British white paper on the reorganization of the foreign service of the United Kingdom. Many of the problems with which we are faced here are similar to those for which Mr. Eden and his associates have tried to find solutions. I am not sure that there is any solution that is really satisfactory during the war. But we shall continue our efforts and anything that members of the house can suggest which will assist us to meet our needs, both current and prospective, will be most gratefully received.
Before concluding my comments on this subject I should like to say just a word about one of the questions asked by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser). The hon. member will see I have had him in mind right along. On May 5 he asked: "Who is in charge of Latin American affairs in the Department of External Affairs?" The Department of External Affairs is, of course, organized in such a way as to give certain officers definite duties in designated fields. In some cases these fields are based on geographic divisions; in others-questions of international law are an obvious example- they are defined according to subject classifications. The work of all the officers in the department, however, is subject to the review and decision of the under-secretary and ultimately of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Thus it cannot be said that any policy or official action of the department is the responsibility of any specified officer, nor can it properly be said that any officer is "in charge of" any particular field. Thus the only

War Appropriation-External Affairs
fair answer that could be given to the hon. member's question would be that the undersecretary is in charge of Latin American affairs, as he is of all other aspects of departmental activity and that he in turn is under the direction of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is finally responsible, subject, of course, to review by parliament for the conduct of our external relations. Under these circumstances I feel that it would be improper to name any individual or individuals in the department as being responsible for or in charge of any specific aspect of departmental activities.

The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked some questions on Friday last, as reported on page 4596 of Hansard, and I wonder if the Prime Minister could answer them at this time because the hon. member is unavoidably absent from the house to-night on important business: I quote as follows:
"Are members of the military or naval forces of the United States of America who are present in Canada with the consent of the government of Canada for purposes of military operations in connection -with or related to the state of war now existing exempt from criminal proceedings prosecuted in Canadian criminal courts and, if so, to what extent and in what circumstances?"
The stand taken by the United States is that their troops in our country are not subject to the criminal law. There is, however, another matter which I think requires interpretation from the Minister for External Affairs, namely, in connection with a United States order that was issued on June 7, 1943. It is singularly of interest that this order should have been made, and I want to ask whether or not it applies to Canadians or British subjects who are employed by contractors in connection with work on the Alaska highway I quote:

War Appropriation-External Affairs
"Paragraph 1 of Northwest Service Command General Orders No. 23, dated June 7, ,1943, subject:	'United States military jurisdiction
over civilians in Northwest Service Command' is quoted for the information of all concerned:
'Regardless of citizenship, civilian employees of the United States government, or of contractors, working under and in physical proximity to the United States army, including those United States citizens in the above categories discharged from their employment who are awaiting transportation to the United States, are subject to military law and discipline under Article of War 2 (d)'."
Does that mean that Canadians who are working for contractors under or in proximity to the United States army in Canada are subject only to military law?
The hon. member points out that this question has been raised by civilians who find themselves in this category.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question
asked by the hon. member was referred to the legal adviser of the Department of External Affairs and I have in my hand the reply which he has prepared.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asks:
Does that mean that Canadians who are working for contractors under or in proximity to the United States army in Canada are subject only to military law?
Canadians working for contractors under such circumstances are not subject only to military law.
As a matter of fact, the position taken by the Canadian government is that such persons, whether Canadians or not, are subject to Canadian law. In the United Kingdom persons in this position are ordinarily subject only to the United States military courts in criminal matters. The only exception is that persons who are not United States citizens do not come within the scope of the legislation unless they enter into their employment outside of the United States.
The position of contractors and their employees has not been referred to the supreme court for consideration. Some authorities take the view that persons who are subject to the military law of a visiting force are exempt from the local criminal jurisdiction, notwithstanding that they are not members of the force. This, however, is a view which has not received the support of the Canadian government.
Mr. GRAYrDON: I think this item is one which provides an opportunity for me to seek some information from the Prime Minister with respect to the relationship of the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of External Affairs. As far as our present
and prospective relations, diplomatic and commercial, with South America are concerned, it has been made abundantly clear during the debate that keen and increasing interest is shown by Canadians in the countries of Central and South America. I daresay that if the war should conclude within a reasonable time, more Canadians would be planning to visit south and central American republics than almost any other place in the world, so great is the interest in the southern portion of this continent. This of course should have its reflection in the policy pursued by the government. It has been rumoured from time to time that there may be some amalgamation or other change of relationship between the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is difficult for a layman to understand how two departments can operate hand in hand without very close relationship in respect of their personnel and the manner in which they carry on their business. Can the Prime Minister give the committee some information on this subject, particularly as it relates to the operations of the departments in the central and south American countries?
I should like to supplement this question with an inquiry whether there is in contemplation any overhaul of or extensive change with regard to, the Department of External Affairs. I notice with some interest that the jurisdiction of the parliamentary assistant to the president of the privy council, to judge from the terms of his appointment, does not cover the Department of External Affairs.
If there is to be an extension of relationships, as to both diplomacy and trade, with the central and south American republics and other nations, it would seem to me that the old structure of the Department of External Affairs, operating in one compartment, and the old structure of the Department of Trade and Commerce, operating in another, might properly be the subject of a complete overhaul to bring the two departments up to date to meet modern conditions and to prevent, in line with the Prime Minister's statement, a considerable strain upon the personnel of these two departments.
In making these remarks I am not casting any reflection on the personnel of the Department of External Affairs. I think the Prime Minister could clarify the attitude of the government and explain what it has in contemplation with respect to making these departments into a working whole, to the benefit and advancement of our relationships with the countries to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not in his seat at the moment, and I shall have to be a little careful of what I say about his department.
I believe, however, he will agree with me that it is most desirable that the two departments should work in the closest possible, not merely harmony, but relationship. But I do not think it would be desirable from the public point of view that the two departments should at any time be merged into one. It is true that each of them operates to a certain extent in similar areas, but there is a distinct difference between the field which has to do with the political side of public affairs in the large sense of the word, the relationship between the governments of different countries on a multitude of subjects, and that which has to do with distinctively commercial and business affairs.
They are pretty closely related, nevertheless.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The commercial side is merely one phase of the work. Trade and commerce has been recognized since the time of confederation as being deserving of a separate department of government with a responsible minister, just as the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Mines and Resources might be. As a matter of fact, it would not be wise that the gentlemen in the capitals of the different states who have to do with diplomatic affairs generally should also be expected to look after the commercial interests of the country.
I never heard that suggested seriously.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That they
should? No, I thought not. But there are always along the way cases arising where the Department of Trade and Commerce would find it absolutely necessary, for the pursuit of its own business in a foreign country, to have very' close relations with the representatives of the Department of External Affairs. I recall many years ago Canada had a business or commercial representative in Japan; I think he was Mr. Preston. He was a representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce in Japan. The then government of Japan would not receive him because he had not diplomatic standing. It was held by the government there, according to diplomatic practice, that the government itself could only be conferred with -if I may use that expression-by one who carried the status necessary to that purpose. The ramifications of the work of the Department of External Affairs are such that one finds so many matters which require the attention of that department that it would
I Mr. G ray don. ]
not be possible to join the two. I would say, however, that for some time the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of External Affairs have been conferring together to see to what extent it would be possible to make their relationships serve each other's purposes to'a greater degree than they do at the present time, each to facilitate the other's work in as large a measure as possible.
My hon. friend has referred to the fact that there was an appointment of parliamentary assistant to the president of the council and not to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. May I take advantage of this moment to explain why, to put it in a direct way, I myself have retained the position of Minister of External Affairs while holding the office of Prime Minister at this time of war. I can assure hon. members, and my' hon. friend in particular, that it has not been through any desire on my part to carry the extra portfolio. I would point- out that in time of war nine-tenths of the Prime Minister's work is related to external affairs, and it would be making his task in some ways more difficult were he to try to assume the responsibility of the office of Prime Minister without being responsible as well for external affairs, when practically every decision of vital importance at this time, which has to be made by the Prime Minister, is one that is related to external affairs or would have to come as a recommendation from a minister of external affairs.
I am perhaps stating this in an exaggerated way, but it is impossible to separate the two at this time, and the more so in Canada for the reason that they have never been separated. The Department of External Affairs originated under Sir Wilfrid Laurier's administration, Sir Joseph Pope being the first deputy minister, and from that time to the present the two offices have been actually working together as one, so much so that the Prime Minister gets no appropriation from parliament and what he receives in the way of salary comes to him from external affairs. Matters of bookkeeping and many other things of the Prime Minister's office are managed by external affairs. The two have been carried on, on the business side, pretty much exclusively by the Department of External Affairs.
In not appointing an assistant to the Minister of External Affairs, I have not lost sight of the fact that I am in daily contact with my colleagues, and my colleagues, particularly those who are members of the war committee of the cabinet, are the ones immediately concerned with matters relating to external affairs, so that they are in a position to assist

War Appropriation-External Affairs
me, as in. fact they do. They carry much of the responsibility that I have to assume in that particular position.
There have been placed under the war committee and under the cabinet as a whole, which is presided over by the president of the council, a number of new boards that have recently been appointed, such as the wartime information board. I mention that as one of the most prominent. It is not possible for any minister to keep track of the work of these different boards. There are different heads and chairmen of the boards, but I felt it was desirable to have someone who would be careful to exercise supervision over that aspect of the work, and for that and other reasons I thought it desirable to appoint a special parliamentary assistant to the president of the privy council.
I could enlarge upon what I have said, but I hope I have made clear to the committee that at this time it would be practically impossible to separate the two offices. I think they should be separated, and I hope I may have something to do with seeing that they are; but so long as the war continues I am afraid it will be necessary to keep them together.
I might point out this fact. Australia, as was mentioned by some hon. member, has established a department of external affairs. New Zealand has just done the same. The Prime Minister of New Zealand, Mr. Fraser, has recently telegraphed me that he himself will feel it necessary to hold the portfolio of minister of external affairs. I can understand that. Hon. members will appreciate the situation.

I may supplement the question I asked by saying this. I think there is justifiable curiosity on the part of the public and of members of this house as to why the parliamentary assistant was given to the president of the privy council, because that did not seem to most of us to be the heavy end of the Prime Minister's department. He has mentioned the wartime information board, and I quite share with him the view that that in itself would not ease the burden that anyone would have to carry, as has perhaps been duly indicated by the discussions in the house. But in addition to that, it does seem to me that if a parliamentary assistant were needed, he was needed more perhaps in the Department of External Affairs than in the office of the president of the privy council, which seemed to be the very much lighter duty, and that prompted my inquiry in the first instance, because I have heard that suggestion made in several quarters since the appointment was made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I hope that
neither the house nor the parliamentary assistant himself will attempt to construe his functions as so definitely limited that he does not go outside of what immediately comes under the president of the privy council. As my hon. friend- knows, practically all government boards have to be kept more or less under review by the president of the council. There is not one of these boards that at this particular time is not concerned with some aspect of external relations. The war information board, for example might almost be described as carrying on a task more for the Minister of External Affairs than for the president of the council, because it is largely concerned with war information in other countries. It has a phase of work related to Canada, but a very large part of its -work is the dissemination of information in regard to Canada's war effort in the United States, Britain, Australia and other countries. I might mention other boards having similar obligations. Nearly everything that has grown up in the period of the war relates in some way to external affairs, but the boards themselves come more immediately under the purview of the cabinet, and a part of the parliamentary assistant's duties, as he was told when he undertook the task, is to take on anything referred to him by the Prime Minister.

He is a sort of roving
commission, in other words.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is a very necessary person to have near at hand in times like the present, and may I say that he has been an exceedingly helpful and able assistant.

I, too, was surprised
that when the assistant to the Prime Minister was appointed he was not appointed as assistant to the ministry of external affairs, because it has always seemed to me that the foreign policy of this country required very careful attention by this parliament and that the Prime Minister was giving personal attention to matters about which the house and the country were not well informed. I have in mind the fact that Canada is a small country; yet Canada has played a very important role in this war; and there are many small countries playing important roles in the war, some of which are rather disturbed because they think the major powers, particularly the two English-speaking powers, tend to decide things without sufficient reference to the other members of the united nations and particularly the smaller powers.



War Appropriation-External Affairs
Those of us who have attended various unofficial conferences in the last year, where we have met representatives of countries that might be regarded as small, have become painfully aware of that fact, and one of the interesting things to me has been that Canada is the small country to which they look as spokesman for the whole group of smaller nations. I think that is particularly true because we are English-speaking and many of the smaller countries do not speak the language we speak, while the two great powers, the United States and Great Britain, both speak that language.
Then, too, there have been certain disturbing events: our absence from some of the conferences; the fact that we have not been invited to some of the conferences; the fact that so much has been decided merely by conference between the Prime Minister of Great Britain, whom we all admire, and the great President of the United States. Nonetheless these two countries are only two of the major powers involved in this war. Ever since last autumn when North Africa was invaded-I said something about this the other afternoon- there has been a great deal of discussion of the situation in North Africa, and I want to ask the Prime Minister what our relation is, if any, to the French committee of national liberation. It has been recognized by some of the smaller nations, by Norway, Belgium and some other countries, as the spokesman for France. Yet undoubtedly there is a feeling abroad, and I am free to confess that I share that feeling, that far too much authority has been assumed by the state department of our powerful neighbour to the south. Indeed, in Great Britain, if you follow the British press carefully, you will read a number of articles developing that particular thought and expressing grave concern that if the same kind of policy that was apparent last autumn in North Africa is carried forward into Italy and is attempted also in France when it is liberated, there will be grave danger of discontent leading subsequently to an upheaval in Europe and perhaps even to another world war on different lines from the one in which we are now engaged. I should like to know what our policy is in relation to some of these important matters. What is our relationship, if any, to the French committee of liberation? What should be our attitude regarding the policy pursued by the state department of the United States in relation to the situation in North Africa? Are we as a parliament satisfied with that? Are we prepared to allow the same kind of policy, namely collaboration, not with

Mussolini any more than with Petain, but collaboration nevertheless with people who were very close to the nazi-controlled regime in France or in other countries?
Even now there are suggestions that we might find in Italy persons who have been pretty close to Mussolini, but who are to-day not as close to him and who might head a new government in Italy. There is a good deal of discussion abroad as to what is going to happen in Europe if these near-quislings are to be recognized, and of whether instead we are to recognize the leaders who to-day are very largely underground but are conducting a great struggle against the nazi regime at the risk of their lives. I do not intend to enter into the relative merits of General Giraud and General de Gaulle, because they are together now on the French committee of national liberation and, superficially at least, that committee is functioning with both of them on it. I hope they will remain together. I hope the committee will function under the leadership of these two famous Frenchmen. At the same time I felt that I should ask the Prime Minister what consideration has been given to these problems, and what is the view of Canada in regard to the future of committees of this sort and of the desirability of collaboration with persons who to-day are either leading underground movements in Europe or the undesirability of choosing persons or committees from among the former friends of the regimes we hope to overthrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend mentioned that several small countries had given recognition to the national committee of liberation.
Also Russia, I believe.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was going to say that he did not draw to the attention of the committee the fact that the larger powers, the United Kingdom and the United States, are not among the countries that thus far have recognized the national committee.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In like manner, thus far Canada has not given immediate recognition for reasons that I will make clear in a moment. We have welcomed every move that indicated that the forces under the control of General de Gaulle and those under General Giraud were drawing closer together and that these groups were coming to a common understanding on matters of important policy. We have felt that it would be unwise to take any steps which, if taken

War Appropriation-External Affairs
prematurely might be wrongly interpreted by one or the other of these groups. We believed that it would not be long before the position would be so clear that there would be no doubt at all as to the proper moment for recognition.
I might say that Mr. Dupuy, who has been counsellor to our legation to the governments in London from the occupied countries, has recently been in North Africa. The department asked him to go to North Africa and stay there for a time to size up the situation and give us the benefit of his immediate knowledge as well as his wide experience when we came to discuss the matter in a more final way. He is now in Canada.
The committee will have noticed that General Giraud will be here on Thursday of this week, and we have felt, knowing that General Giraud was coming to Canada, that we would wish to have a conversation with him about the situation before taking any steps.
We have had a representative in Ottawa, as my hon. friend knows, of the de Gaullists. We have been following the situation closely from both sides, and it will not, I think, be long before it will be perfectly eviden which is the right moment at which to give recognition to the French committee on national liberation. The government will take its action at that time.

If I may ask a supplementary question, does the Prime Minister consider that it is in conformity with the policies of democratic countries-I will put it this way, of our own democratic country, which is the only one involved, that the French national committee of liberation should be virtually under the control of a United ' States general in the field? My information is, and I may say that it has come from British sources, that this has caused a great deal of misgivings in the underground movement in France itself, and I think one can understand that feeling. I should like to know the Prime Minister's view of that particular wray of handing the French situation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would say to my hon. friend that this committee has two chairmen, each one of whom is a Frenchman, General Giraud and General de Gaulle, and I do not think I would be helping the situation at all by seeking to cast reflections on one or the other.
Mr. COLDW'ELL: I did not mean that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But the form in which my hon. friend's question is put makes it pretty difficult for me to answer it without doing that. I do not think he so intended.
No, I did not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Similarly my hon. friend asked me if I thought a certain policy of the United States state department was correct. I do not think it is for a member of the Canadian government to reflect on policies of the government of another country.

I did not intend to reflect on the state department of the United States, or on the fact that General Eisenhower practically had the right to approve this committee. I did not mean that. I believe that as one of the united nations we must frankly face, either here or in a closed session, some of the implications of this whole situation. I can see that we are going to be in the same situation as we were before the war when we had no independent policy, no policy of our own. I think that is true, and by following the line of least resistance we allowed our influence to be unused, when it could have been used in a more constructive way. I am anxious to see that we do not fall into that position again.

Mr. Chairman, I find it difficult to follow the line of argument of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Because our present relations in North Africa are so delicate, I can see no useful purpose being served by discussing them in any great detail in the House of Commons.
That is the old story.

That may be a good answer from my hon. friend's point of view, but I think the public generally will have some sympathy for the position I take. I refer now to his statement with respect to General Eisenhower's position in the North African theatre of war. I think everyone has to recognize that this is something more than a political matter; it is a military matter as well, and one which is fraught with all kinds of possibilities, particularly so at a time when we are beginning an offensive which has given us a foothold on European soil. I do feel at this time that no useful purpose can be served by discussing at this long distance the matters which were raised. In saying that, I do not desire to reflect in an unfriendly way upon my hon. friend.

War Appropriation-External Affairs
I take it from the Prime Minister's remarks that our position as Canadians in the North African political situation is this: we are taking whatever steps are necessary in collaboration with the United States and Great Britain, and we are working in close harmony with them. I should be surprised to hear that that was not the situation. I should like to have assurance from the Prime Minister that the matter is being carefully and harmoniously worked out, having in mind with regard to both the military and the political situation the other great powers who are interested with us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say to my hon. friend that right along, by that I mean ever since North Africa came into the picture, there has been the closest collaboration between our government and the British government and our government and the United States government with respect to all the questions that were likely to be of common concern; and certainly this one is foremost among the number.

Mr. Chairman, last Friday
night at eleven o'clock the hon. member for Yale asked the Prime Minister if he intended to reply to the speech of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi before the item in committee is passed, or if he will make his speech on another item. The answer of the Prime Minister was as follows:
I have been making notes of the various points raised. I shall try to get them in order between now and the beginning of next week, and may endeavour to answer them all pretty much at the same time.
We appear to be drawing toward the close of this long drawn-out debate, and I was wondering if the Prime Minister would make any statement in answer to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was hoping I would feel sure enough of my ground after one day's discussion to take up, in concluding the discussion, the different points that had been raised, but up to this moment I have not been any too sure it is at an end. However, I had no intention of overlooking the questions which were asked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and which were asked again this afternoon by the hon. member for Kootenay West. The question was as to what the government proposed to do with respect to the Japanese nationals in this country when the war was over, whether we would see that they returned to Japan. First of all I thank my hon. friend for the implied compliment that this government will be necessarily in office when the war is over and will have to do

with post-war matters. I should like to oblige him at once by telling him what the government's policy at that time will be; but what I would say to him as to what the government's policy at that time will be will depend upon the times, as they may be, and upon what the situation may be at that moment. My hon. friend will realize we have to-day as one of our allies the United States of America; that in dealing with all matters relating to the Pacific our two countries have been keeping very closely in touch with each other. I should rather hestitate at this moment, without either the war being concluded or an opportunity of conference with governments of allies, to make a pronouncement upon war policies which affect the whole of the oriental situation. I do not think that I should be expected to do so or that it would be wise to do so. May I give a very clear reason as to why it would be unwise to make a pronouncement of the kind.
The hon. member for Kootenay West this afternoon said that if we reached the time where Japan saw that she was getting the better of the situation, some of the Japanese nationals in Canada might cause a good deal of trouble and we would have a good deal of difficulty with them. He said at the present time they were not causing any embarrassment. I cannot imagine that we are going to come to a time where Japan will be justified in assuming that she will have the last word in this war. I am pretty certain that she will not. However, take the present situation. At the present time, according to what the hon. member has said, the situation is quiescent, or at least there is no difficulty arising because of the Japanese in this country. But I ask the hon. member what the situation would be to-morrow if I were to make a pronouncement to-day which would be of the character that the hon. member for Comox-Albemi would wish me to make. Does he think we would be able to handle the situation within Canada itself as well from now to the end of the war as we are able to do to-day, and as we have dealt with it thus far. I do not believe I can say more than that. When the time comes, if the government is in office we shall certainly have a policy that will be very clear; it will be a policy that will be the result of mature consideration with those that we believe should be consulted meanwhile, and it will be made known at the right time to the country.

I should like to ask the
Prime Minister if the papers dealing with the international stabilization of currency will be

dealt with at this time, or whether they should be dealt with when the estimates of the Minister of Finance are before the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think stabilization of currency would come more appropriately under the heading of finance than under any other heading.

I was a little bit surprised at the Prime Minister's answer to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni with respect to the policy relating to the Japanese situation. There is a feeling across Canada that this is a Canadian problem rather than a British Columbia problem alone. I am not desirous, as the Prime Minister knows, of raising questions that will embarrass the government in the handling of delicate problems, because I believe such a course is inexcusable at all times, but I believe that the Prime Minister ought to make it clear whether or not the policy of not declaring the government's intention with respect to the Japanese population in Canada is dictated from fear with respect to the internal situation of Canada in regard to the Japanese, or whether it is dictated by some influence it may have on the Japanese with respect to reprisals on the part of the Japanese empire. I do not want to press the Prime Minister unnecessarily on this point. I do not want to take upon myself the job of urging him to take a position that will in any way jeopardize our position as a nation or interfere with our security. But I do believe there is a strong and ever-growing body of public opinion in Canada that is asking the government to deal in some direct way with the Japanese problem which was raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I do not think the Prime Minister's answer to him will be received with the kind of approbation in Canada that a forthright statement of policies would bring from the people. I quite understand the Prime Minister will not agree with me when I say that this kind of statement has some elements of appeasement in it. I do not wish to convey that idea unnecessarily to him. Nevertheless there will be a great section in this country who will believe that it has many of the elements or factors of appeasement in it. I think in these times, if we as a nation cannot make a definite statement with respect to enemy populations within our gates, while a war is on, then it will be more difficult to persuade governments to take forthright steps when peace comes. As I say, I do not wish unnecessarily to press the point. Nevertheless I think the Prime Minister ought to know that there is quite a strong body of public opinion
in Canada which feels that the government ought to make some forthright declaration on the point.

Before the Prime Minister answers, I should like to ask him whether he realizes the natural anxiety in the minds of those people in the southern part of British Columbia, where three-quarters of the Japanese removed from the protected area now are. They are in camps, in these empty towns which have been fitted up for them. They are in work camps in outlying places. People in the southern part of British Columbia, east of the protected area, now find themselves the recipients of 18,000 Japanese. They realize that the people in the protected area will not look with equanimity on the return of the Japanese to that part. They know that the agreements with the three provinces which have received Japanese contain a clause to the effect that the Japanese shall be removed. The people whom I represent see the danger of these Japanese being returned to that part of British Columbia where there are already 18,000 of them. I wonder if the Prime Minister realizes what I call the natural anxiety of those people, and whether he will consider making a statement which would tend to relieve that natural anxiety.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Answering the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) first. The government has already made it clear that it was appreciated that the bringing of a number of Japanese into these ghost towns, so-called, was naturally creating a situation which would not be regarded as pleasant or desirable if it were a continuing one, and that an effort would be made to see that that situation was relieved as early as possible. That was clear, and the government of course will hold to that. The arrangements made internally have been made to meet the existing emergent situation in the best and quickest possible way. They have never been intended as permanent arrangements, and certainly those communities most affected at the present time ought to be and, I believe will be, first considered when the time comes that it is possible to help relieve the situation.
Then, may I say to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) that when he talks about appeasement I am afraid he is using a word in its application to the situation now existing between Japan and Canada the full significance of which he possibly has not appreciated. I assure my hon. friend this government has done nothing with any desire to appease the Japanese. But I ask him, and I ask his colleagues whether he or they believe
