a pronouncement on my part to-night which would indicate a vindictive attitude on the part of Canada toward Japanese nationals in this country would be welcomed by Canadians who are prisoners of war in Japan at this time. I ask him whether such a pronouncement would be welcomed by Canadian civilians who are now in Japan. It is very easy to proceed in a light-hearted way to condemn the government for not coming out and making this or that pronouncement, without so much as considering what the effect of such a pronouncement might be. It may be all very well to have one's mind on politics in British Columbia, but to forget the effect of politics in the whole of Canada, in a wartime situation such as we have at present is a serious matter.
Does the right hon. gentleman say that I had in mind politics in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. I say that the mere mention of appeasement to-day is to use a word which is used for political purposes. It is not used1 for the public good.

I rise to a point of order. May I say to the Prime Minister that I felt in rising on this point that I was taking perhaps as reasonable a stand with the Prime Minister as one man could with another. So far as appeasement is concerned, may I say that I used the word with the feeling that there would be a section of the country who would regard it as an appeasement policy. And more than that, I think if my right hon. friend would recall my words he must admit that his reply wras quite unwarranted. I had no thoughts in the matter, except that there are many people, in fact a great section of our people in Canada, who feel that some forthright declaration should be made by the Prime Minister. I asked the Prime Minister to reply, but I told him particularly that I was not urging or pressing him if indeed there was some question of public security involved.
I thought I was being just as fair as anyone could possibly be under the circumstances.
I do not wish the Prime Minister to undertake to place insinuations cn matters I discuss.
I raised the matter, not with the thought of politics in British Columbia, or politics anywhere else across the whole Dominion of Canada. I do not wish the Prime Minister to insinuate unfairly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I say to my hon. friend that he knows as well as I the significance attaching in the public mind to the word " appeasement." He knows how the 
public view a charge of appeasement against a government in this time of war. And if he did not wish to be misunderstood he should have chosen his word more carefully. However, I am quite prepared to drop the matter there. I have made it clear, I think, first of all that there will be time enough to state what the government's post-war policy is when the war is won. I do not think the government should be expected at this time, when we are seeking to win a war, and have very close relationships with our allies in different parts of the worlds to make pronouncements without even a conference with them, when the situation is one' which might affect them as well as ourselves. We should not be called upon or be expected to make pronouncements of policy which have not been considered in relation to the time and the situation to which they will relate. That is only common sense in the business of government. I think the public will see the reasonableness of that position.
I do hope I have made it clear, as the committee well knows, that there are a number of our own Canadian soldiers to-day in prison camps in Japan. Also a number of our civilians are in that country. And I ask the committee whether in those circumstances hon. members believe it would be in the interest of Canada and in the interest of her men who have fought overseas and become prisoners of war, to make a pronouncement which might only serve to inflame the Japanese mind.

The Prime Minister's
remarks partly answer the question I asked. If he will recall, I asked whether or not it was a question of an internal condition which prompted the government not to make a declaration, and whether there was any question of reprisals over there. If it is on the latter basis then, as the Prime Minister indicated, is that the only basis upon which the government is actually proceeding in connection with this line of policy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have given two or three statements already. I said it is not on general grounds. I do not think a government that is governed by common sense would attempt to make pronouncements with respect to hypothetical situations. When we know what the situation is that we have to face, we will deal with it in the light of existing conditions.
That would really do away with the question of post-war planning so far as the government is concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: What progress has been made in the negotiations leading to a further exchange of Canadian and Japanese nationals? I understand that last year between forty and fifty Japanese were returned in exchange for Canadians. On two or three occasions during the present session a similar question has been placed on the order paper, and in each case the answer has been that negotiations are under way. I should like the Prime Minister to tell us the situation at the present time with regard to these negotiations. Would he tell us also the approximate number of Japanese nationals in Canada who have signified a wish to be exchanged during the war? I believe that quite a few have asked to be sent back, and it would be interesting to know the approximate number. A second question has to do with a statute passed in 1913 known as the Japanese Treaty Act, which really made Canada a party to a treaty between Great Britain and Japan. In one of the articles of the treaty there is a provision for termination on notice, after a certain lapse of time. I presume the fact that we are at war would cancel the agreement, but I do not know whether it would repeal the statute. There is certain British Columbia legislation which has been held to be ultra vires because of this dominion statute known as the Japanese Treaty Act. I should like to know if consideration has been given to having this act repealed. It would seem to me that that is a step which should be taken. Finally, now that we are at war with Japan, would it be possible to have the Lemieux agreement tabled in the house? As the Prime Minister knows, this agreement was negotiated with Japan in 1907 or 1908, and I think he personally had something to do with the negotiations. It has never been tabled and I am wondering whether thore is any reason why it should not be now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In regard to
the exchange of nationals, I understand that a second ship is leaving Japan shortly, if it has not already done so. It will be bringing some Canadian nationals back to Canada and will be taking Japanese nationals back to Japan.

How many are going back
from Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I cannot say offhand. I am informed that the one ship is not only for Canada, but is also for the
United States and certain South American countries. The second repatriation party is expected to leave this summer, returning Japanese from Canada, the United States and South America. That is the information I have and I cannot give more than that. As to the number who have applied, I would ask that this question stand and I shall try to get the information. In connection with treaties, war puts an end to them. I am not sufficient of a legal authority to say offhand whether the provisions of a statute which relates to these matters would simultaneously be regarded as coming to an end, but I shall endeavour to get definite information on that point. I certainly think in effect it would be at an end; if it is not, there would appear to be no reason why it should not be repealed.
The difficulty is that it makes certain British Columbia legislation invalid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has raised the question and I shall have it looked into. I do not see any reason why the Lemieux agreement should not be tabled. I shall endeavour to get the particulars and have them tabled.
Could we have the estimated number of Canadian nationals now in Japan? The Prime Minister may not have this information at the moment, but perhaps he would not mind getting it if it is available.

I think it is about 9,000, if my hon. friend wishes to know. The Japanese in Canada are divided roughly into three. One-third are nationals still subjects of Japan; the second third are nationals who have been naturalized, and the third third are Japanese who have been born in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman is giving the number of Japanese in Canada; the leader of the opposition asked for the number of Canadian nationals in Japan.

Like the leader of the opposition, I feel a sense of grievance at being accused in the language of the Prime Minister that any suggestion as to methods of dealing with this important subject should be put down to the cheapest form of political intrigue, or even worse than that, the suggestion that we are almost, if not wholly disloyal in connection with the steps to be taken for the carrying on of the war and the subsequent peace. The Prime Minister tells us that it is against common sense to look forward to what we should do in certain given circumstances.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend must not misconstrue what I have said. I did not say that it was not common sense. to look forward to what should be done. Those were not my words at all. I spoke about stating a definite policy with reference to a situation which one did not know at the present time and could not say what it might be.

There is really not much difference between the interpretation I put on it and the language of the Prime Minister, although his words may be more dignified. In planning an election, what is the first thing every party gets out? They get out a platform. What is that platform but a declaration of policy which, if returned to power, they are prepared to carry out. The Liberals formulated a platform, I think in 1919, and so far as I know, that platform is still being carried out, or it is supposed to be. From time to time reference is made to it. It is a long time from 1919 to 1943, and if we are still following that platform as a chart laid down in 1919, there must have been men of great vision in those days who could foresee and lay down a definite policy that would be followed out so many years in the future.
I have been associated with this question of the Japanese for many years, and I certainly do not like the suggestion that I am animated by the cheapest sense of political ambition. I am occasionally accused of that in the press, but I think I can leave it to my constituents and to my province to decide whether that accusation is justified. The Prime Minister has said that our nationals who are in Japan may suffer if suggestions similar to those which I have expressed at different times are carried out. But what should be considered is the difference between the oriental and the occidental mind. The Prime Minister thinks that if our dealings are fair, if we do not do anything unjust to the Japanese, in the same spirit they will treat our men over there in a similar manner.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that. I never said the Japanese would treat our men fairly; I said they might be very much more vindictive than they are-which is a very different thing.

Well, I was putting it on the right side: if we treated them decently they would treat us decently. Now the Prime Minister says he did not say this; he said, if we did not take care we would be subject to reprisals-if you will allow me to use that word.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I did not.

Well, then, it would be the worse for our prisoners in Japan if we indicated what our policy was going to be. Here I come down to the difference between the occidental and the oriental. All that Japan would gather from any action of that kind, supposing we said, "Now, we are going to give you Japs everything after the war," would be that we are afraid of them. The oriental's mind works like that; he would say, "We can do anything we like to our Canadian prisoners, because these people are afraid of us." If the Prime Minister took a bold stand and said, "We are going to do thus and so"; and if he has any suspicion of reprisals, he could add the pronounced warning that we, the people of Canada, wall definitely punish those people who have not treated our men according to the recognized usage of prisoners of war; that would come home to the Jap. If the Jap thinks he is going to be punished he will be very much more careful about what he does than if you tell him that you will treat him as a gentleman and expect him to act as a gentleman. I make that very clear, and heaven knows I am the last to do anything which would imperil our men over there. But I sincerely believe that a policy of indefiniteness-for I do not want to use offensive language-will hurt our men over there, because it will convince the Japanese mind that Japan can afford to play fast and loose with us, whereas were he boldly and definitely warned, as long ago the United States warned Germany, and it would have been becoming for us to have warned Japan at the very first suggestion of impropriety-warned as to what the international rules of the Geneva convention required, and that if they were not adhered to to their utmost extent, there would be, not reprisals, but punishments accruing after the war to those who directly and indirectly were responsible,
I am convinced that that point of view and that action would appeal more to their mentality than any suggestion of soft-pedalling our rights in the hope of influencing them favourably. I cannot remember the author of the poem, but there is a verse running in my mind something like this:
Still the bold brave man is fortunate He keeps his object ever full in sight;
True t'is a narrow way that leads to bliss But right before there is no precipice.
Fear makes men look aside And so their footing miss.
Courage and boldness should be our policy, not expediency.

I have no sympathy with the people who want to appease Japan; in fact I have been more than a little disturbed when I have heard statements made that perhaps after the war a strong Japan in the far east may be a useful counterbalance in Asia. We should make it very clear to the Japanese that any atrocities committed on our nationals in Japan at the present time will be punished to the utmost of our power when the war is over; I believe the effect would be beneficial.
But I rose to say two things: this is one of them. I heard a very wise Chinese gentleman say a few months ago that we-that is the United States and Canada-had placed one of the finest propaganda weapons in the hands of the Japanese by our treatment of the Japanese in Canada and the United States during this war; that over the air from Tokyo to the people of the east went the story that these people in North America had torn up the roots of people, some of whom had been born of Japanese parentage in these countries, that we had taken their property away from them, and had placed them in internment camps, whereas German nationals and Italian nationals of the second and third generation had not been so treated; and over the air from Japan went the story, "that is because these people are of a different colour." There was the racial angle placed in the hands of the Japanese war lords to use as an effective propaganda weapon. Therefore I can see the point made by the Prime Minister to-night. We should, it seems to me, make it very clear that we are out to destroy Japanese power once and for all, that when this war is over we are going to punish those upon whom we can lay our hands who are responsible for any atrocities, but to my mind we should be careful lest we raise an issue in Asia which may be very difficult for us to meet in the future and moreover may interfere with our winning over of the Asiatic populations to our side during the war.
The other thing I rose to say was that a short time ago we had a visit in this chamber from a very charming lady, the wife of the Generalissimo of China, and when she was speaking to this house my mind ran over the situation in this country both before the war and at the present time. I happen to have to-night with me a dispatch which was filed by the Canadian Press as long ago as November 15, 1937, from Brussels. Hon. members will recollect that in October, 1937, a conference was held at Brussels regarding the situation in China, to give China moral support. At that time the Chinese delegation issued a
statement. A part of that statement refers to Canada. I am going to remind the committee of what it was:
Canada has been a substantial contributor to Japan's weapon of war, according to a statement issued by the Chinese delegation to the nine-power treaty conference to-day.
The statement analyses Japan's dependence on foreign supplies for raw materials. It says that in 1936 Japan imported aluminum, used in aircraft manufacture, valued at 12 million yen ($3,480,000). Of this Canada furnished 71-7 per cent.
In the same year Japan imported 33 million yen worth of copper, of which Canada furnished 97-11 per cent.
In the same pa pet there followed a comparative table issued from Ottawa showing the increases in our sales to Japan last year.
That was 1936. It seems to me that we owe a debt to China. We have supplied her enemy with the wherewithal to make war. A few days ago, on the seventh day of the seventh month, China began her seventh year of war, and during the last six dreary years the Chinese people have suffered terrific casualties. I know, and I believe hon. members know, that wherever we meet educated Chinese ladies or gentlemen, sooner or later the conversation will drift around to the position of the Chinese in North America and in Canada. We have very few Chinese in this country and they are becoming fewer. I believe the time has come when we shall be able to make an agreement with the Chinese government so that there will be no danger of an influx of Chinese into our country. Of course no more are coming in now. It seems to me, therefore, that it would be a very fine gesture at this time on the part of Canada if we said to those Chinese who are in our midst, "We are going to treat you as we treat other people; as a token to your countrymen, we are going to treat you now as we treat all others who have come to us from other countries; thus we are going to give you equal status as Canadian citizens." I say that there is no danger of any influx. They are here. We know that in many respects they have performed useful functions and many of us, particularly those living on the western plains, have received many a kindness from a Chinese restaurant keeper or a Chinese settled in our midst. It seems to me that the sacrifices their country has made might be recognized in this way. I may say that a short time ago in Washington I had the privilege of listening for a few minutes to representations seeking the repeal of the United States exclusion law. We have few Chinese people here, and I suggest to the Prime Minister that some consideration be given

to this manner of showing our appreciation of what the Chinese nation has done for us in its long struggle.

The hon. gentleman is making that suggestion from the federal point of view. Is there any federal legislation or regulation now that takes the vote away from the Chinese or that prevents them from voting in any province?

I think that where provincial legislation exists, as it does in some provinces, our government, recognizing the services that the Chinese have rendered to the democratic nations in this war, might approach the provincial governments with a view to removing these barriers for the few Chinese in this country, thus conferring upon them the rights of full dominion citizenship.

Does the hon.
gentleman suggest the same for the Japanese?

I am not referring to the Japanese. I made my position clear as far as the Japanese are concerned, but my hon. friend knows that their disability is felt very keenly by educated Chinese ladies and gentlemen who come to this country, and when we acclaim the distinguished wife of the head of the Chinese government in this chamber, surely the position that many of our Chinese citizens, as Chinese residents, find themselves in, is at least incongruous.

Can the hon. gentleman really say that there is any resentment among the Chinese against the Dominion of Canada in connection with their lack of the voting privilege in some provinces? There is against the province, but can he say there is any against Canada?
Many of the Chinese fail to understand and to recognize the distinction between the provincial and dominion franchise.
The Chinese in British Columbia have always been without the franchise and they recognize the distinction.
May I tell the hon. member for Cariboo that I am not talking about the Chinese in British Columbia.
But they do recognize the distinction.

I am talking about the Chinese who visit this country, the Chinese one finds around our legations and embassies or who visit Canada. Those are the ones to whom I am referring, not the laundrymen or restaurant keepers one sees in British Columbia, but the educated Chinese gentleman who

feels that his compatriots are not treated as they should be treated by Canada. They fail to make the distinction that the hon. member for Cariboo makes.

What is the benefit of saying in this house something that will confirm the feeling that a resident of China may have, which is wrong, that Canada as a nation is taking the franchise from or refusing to give it to Chinese in Canada? What is the good of making a representation of that kind in this house? His fear is only confirmed.

I have made my position clear. My voice can be heard only in this chamber. I do not speak in the legislature of British Columbia. I am a citizen of Canada. I heard Madame Chiang Kai-shek in this chamber, and I am suggesting to the Prime Minister that approaches might be made by our government to the provinces in which there are disabilities for the removal of those disabilities.
Does that go for the Japanese too?
I made my position clear regarding the Japanese. I am talking about the Chinese, who are our allies, and not about the Japanese, who are our enemies.
With regard to the treatment which it is said we have been according the Japanese'nationals in this country, I do not think we need be unduly perturbed over that.
I hope not.

Anyone who knows anything about the Japanese knows that they themselves inculcate in their children, from the day they are born, right through life, that they are a superior oriental race, distinct and apart. They are the sons of heaven in their own eyes. As I said in my speech the other day, they look down upon us as an inferior race. We need not therefore be perturbed so far as they are concerned. What I wanted to say was this, and I say it with the Prime Minister present. Very often people get up in this country, when some of us undertake to speak about the Japanese and to put before the people the facts as they are, andi immediately tell us what we should do. I repeat that if any of the Japanese born in this country are to remain in this country, the first step that should be taken should be taken by the Japanese themselves; and no Japanese has so far taken the first step in the direction of real Canadian citizenship, for the reason that everyone of them owes allegiance to Japan, whether born in this country or not. We have

War Appropriation-External Affairs
never heard one of them stand up and say to Japan, "You are not our country; we were born here, we are Canadian citizens." I challenge any hon. member to show one instance, in the long life of the Japanese in this country, where one of them has made it apparent that he is a true Canadian citizen.
I was not discussing the Japanese.

I am making a few remarks
along the lines of the speech I made a few nights ago, and I am pointing out to those people who blame us for not doing something for the Japanese, that the Japanese have done nothing themselves in this regard, and until they take the step I suggest-and I speak of those bom in this country-I do not see how we can do anything to make them: truly Canadian. The mere accident of birth does not make them Canadians, though under the law it does. I am speaking of those who owe allegiance to two countries, and I say that no man can be a truly Canadian citizen who owes allegiance in the first instance to Japan, or for that matter to any other country. I was one of those who, in the days before the war, pointed out that we had done a great injustice to the Chinese in excluding them, while at the same time we allowed the Japanese to come in at the rate of 150 a year. I could not see the sense or the righteousness of that, because both are oriental or Mongolian races; and yet we have a Chinese Exclusion Act. I and others as well advocated one for the Japanese, but there were always reasons advanced why we could not do that so far as the Japanese were concerned. Had we done so, our condition would not have been any worse to-day and it might have been better; for, if we had taken a strong stand in those days and said to Japan, "We are closing the door," we would have settled the matter. I may be contradicted in this, but we are following too much the policy of Great Britain. We should settle our own affairs and decide who should settle in this land after the war; and as regards those who are not truly Canadian. citizens, I would say that they should go to the country to which they owe allegiance.

I hope the Prime Minister will fully understand my reference this afternoon to 8,000 Japanese in my own district. I do not know about the reception they have met with in other districts; but I did say that their attitude in Kootenay West was tranquil, but that when the time came and the allies would be devoting their attention
exclusively to Japan, then perhaps that attitude might change and become a dangerous one, particularly where there are so many power plants and bridges nearby. I hope the Prime Minister will not misunderstand our attitude. If he had 8,000 Japanese in Prince Albert and 4,000 recalcitrant Doukhobors, he would feel concerned about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I share the
concern of my hon. friend. I do not say he is wrong in fearing possible consequences from having numbers of Japanese in his community. But I do say that a declaration to-day of the character that I have been asked to make would not help to make the situation any easier. It would make it more difficult.

In justice to a very brave man and a very fine citizen of Japanese origin, I cannot let the statement made by the hon. member for New Westminster go unchallenged1. I have in mind a young Japanese who served with distinction in my own company in France and wffio was decorated by this nation. He saved the life of one of his comrades by performing a very brave deed. He came back and settled in my district where he is now farming and is one of the most highly respected farmers in his particular area. To-day he has two sons serving with the Canadian forces in this war.
While I am on my feet I want to say this with respect to Canada's foreign policy. I could not hope to use the eloquent language used by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George the other day in describing Canada's position and its relationship to the British commonwealth of nations. I was delighted with his address. He is one of the prominent young Liberals of this house, who, given good health, may in the days to come speak with some weight in the councils of the party. I wish to associate myself fully with the interpretation he gave of the place that Canada occupies as a nation and in its very fine relationship to the British commonwealth of nations.
I want to say, too, that we are in the same danger in this country as they were in Great Britain at one period when a group known as Little Englanders arose. We must not be Little Canadians or Little Imperialists. We must be big in our mental approach to the tremendous problems that we shall have to face in the post-war period if we are to justify the fine record we have had in this war. While we think this war period is our great testing time, let us keep in mind that we are all bound together by certain ties of common purpose and that, despite our political differences, that

War Appropriation-External Affairs
tie is there as a moving spirit among the Canadian people. But as we approach victory there is a danger of the tie loosening, as the problems become greater. I view the future with a great deal of concern lest the Canadian people lose some of that unity which is necessary even to approach, let alone solve, the problems that will come to this world when peace is declared.
I wish to put myself on record as saying that Canada's post-war policy in relation to other countries must never be one of hatred or of revenge. It seems to me that if we think in terms of hatred and revenge we shall lose the great opportunity we shall have then to accomplish so much of what we desire to accomplish. Burke's famous statement has lost none of its truth by frequent repetition that in truth you cannot indict a nation, and it will be impossible to indict either Germany or Japan, and this despite all the cruelties and barbarities that Germany and Japan have committed. In our own enlightened self-interest we must keep in mind that there are some seventy millions of human beings living in the Japanese empire and some seventy or more million human beings who call themselves German, and our task will be to find in some way, somehow, a means of educating and training these Germans and Japanese-yes, and Italians-to fit into the new heaven and new earth we speak about. We must have within our own policy the principle of justice rather than of hatred and revenge. I hope that in this house during the war period ive shall be prepared to leave these matters that are bound to create a great deal of controversy to the judgment of the Prime Minister, whose whole history shows his wise tolerance and understanding of the problems with which we are confronted in Canada. I think we can safely assume that he will deal wisely with these problems in their international aspect.
If I may ask a question, what percentage is one out of 25,937?

I might have mentioned an exception, but I remember that Japanese boy who served with me, and I was extremely proud of his record and could not allow the statement of the hon. member for New Westminster to go unchallenged.

The hon. member could probably find more cases than he mentioned, but it seems rather strange that when the Japanese were being removed from the British Columbia coast, and the provincial governments were asked if they would take them, every provincial government, so far as I know, said, 
Yes, we will take them on one condition. That condition was that they would be removed after the war from these other provinces. Are we in British Columbia for ever more to be told that this is simply a British Columbia problem, and when we air our grievances we have it hurled at us that we are Japanese haters, when every province took the stand, we will take these Japanese only if you remove them from our province after the war? If the Japanese are all fine citizens, I would ask the hon. member to explain this stand that was taken by all the provincial governments of Canada.
Would the Prime Minister make a brief statement on the question I raised this afternoon regarding Canada-Newfoundland relations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Before I reply to my hon. friend. I would not like the suggestion that was made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to pass without a word of acknowledgment. May I say that I believe the people of Canada realize that we have had no more gallant ally than we have had in the Chinese, that the sacrifices which the people of China have made in the past seven years have been an immense contribution to the security of this entire continent. Our people have not only come to know but greatly to admire, and, I will go further and say, to have a real affection for the Chinese people. Knowing that, when the government opened a legation in China we expressed to our minister the hope that when he reached Chungking he would explain to the government of China that there were certain difficulties in dealing with the problems which arose between us and the people of China on account of special circumstances in our own country. We asked him to explain the situation very fully and make it perfectly clear that the present administration hoped to be able to work out a solution which would remove any cause on their part to feel that they were being discriminated against as a race.
The Chinese people understand clearly that there is an economic problem of which we on this side have to take full account. Madame Chiang Kai-shek said in my hearing that the Chinese would not misunderstand an arrangement between China and Canada which would take account of the fact that we had certain economic standards which we must carefully preserve. But what she felt was that the Chinese people very much hoped and expected that they would be looked upon by Canadians as people who are entitled to be dealt with

War Appropriation-External Affairs
as equals and not as inferiors. The inference was clear that she hoped some arrangement would be made to remove anything which would cause their people grounds for real offence. I would say that the government is carefully going into these different problems, and I hope that before very long some of the present restrictions, or whatever one may wish to call them, which have been imposed for economic reasons, may be removed, in a way that will take away what of offence there is in them and the economic problem satisfactorily met.
Would the Prime Minister indicate to us what disabilities Madame Chiang Kai-shek mentioned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: One she might have mentioned was exclusion, the nature of the exclusion laws, and I must say I think in that a mistake has been made. Perhaps I should not talk about mistakes being made, but I must say I can see no reason why the Chinese should not have been treated exactly as the Japanese were treated in the matter of the gentlemen's agreement with Japan restricting numbers. I think they were more entitled to an agreement of the kind-certainly in the light of what has happened since the war-than the Japanese were.
Did Madame Chiang Kai-shek give any hint as to the number of Chinese she felt Canada should accept within her boundaries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think Madame Chiang Kai-shek felt that there were many Chinese students who would like to attend our universities, just as Chinese students have been attending universities in the United States, and that there were others who might wish to come for special reasons; that an arrangement which would take cognizance of the fact that there were certain classes or individuals who might come to our country, and that we might send similar classes of our own to their country, would be all to the good of both countries. I believe it should be possible to work out a reciprocal arrangement betweeen Canada and China which would be helpful to both countries.
Can Chinese students not do that now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I remember some years ago trying to make it possible to bring in a number of Chinese students and I encountered great difficulties in the matter.
What was the reason given-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for New Westminster has the floor.
What was the reason given that they were not allowed to come in?

Mr. Chairman, may I suggest to the Prime Minister that in any future policy dealing with the Chinese or the Japanese the problem be not left a British Columbia problem. Too long we have carried the load in this country. We were sneered at for years and years. This is an economic problem as well as a racial one, and in any future policy I would ask the Prime Minister to see that British Columbia is relieved of the burden she has carried for forty years.

Since we are on this Chinese question we may as well see if we can arrive at some sort of agreement in the matter. If the Chinese are to be admitted to this country to live, then the question immediately arises as to how many of them should be admitted. How would you determine the number? Although I have said nothing up to the present time in this house on the problem of the Chinese, yet I have given the matter considerable attention for a good many years. I should be pleased if the Prime Minister would give us some idea as to how far the first lady of China felt we should go in Canada. It is easy to see, if we opened the door to any extent at all, what might happen. China possesses almost four hundred million people. If we allow any considerable number to come to Canada, they would utterly overwhelm us so far as numbers are concerned. 1, should like to get some conception of the extent to which this lady would wish us to go in order that she might feel better about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that the members of this house will be well advised not to attempt to take up too many subjects that might be controversial at this particular time. However carefully hon. members may seek to express their views, there are bound to be certain expressions used which will be misconstrued in some quarters. My hon. friend has just now been referring to questions of millions in China as against small numbers here. That remark when it is read in China to-morrow will sound quite differently to many Chinese ears from what it does to those of us who know my hon. friend and know his heart and his inclinations. I think for that reason, among others, we would be well advised not to get into a general discussion or try to reach final agree-

War Appropriation-External Affairs
ments or settlements at this particular time in a consideration of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs.
I wonder if the Prime Minister would care to answer the question I raised.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will just say the same thing to my hon. friend. While I believe there is a time to consider the question of what is advisable and what may not be advisable with respect to having Newfoundland brought into confederation, this is not the particular moment at which it would be most advisable to discuss the question. As the hon. member knows, the government of Canada is most desirous of preserving the closest possible friendly relations with Newfoundland. We have given expression to our desire in the appointment of a high commissioner of the attainments which he himself has mentioned, in the person of Mr. Burchell. Mr. Burchell has given very careful study to the questions that arise between both the Newfoundland and Canadian governments, Newfoundland and the United States, Newfoundland and Great Britain, and I think he would be the first to say that any discussion with respect to the possible bringing in of Newfoundland to confederation ought to be initiated on the part of the people of Newfoundland rather than on the part of members of this house certainly at this particular time. I took note of what my hon. friend had said, and I prepared with a little care the following words that I thought it might be wise to use if occasion shoidd so demand. I would say that Canadians like and admire the people of Newfoundland. They are attached to them by bonds of sentiment and by the memory of dangers shared and victories won together.-They look forward to a continuation of the friendship and cooperation which have increasingly marked our relations during recent years. Canadians are interested in the defence of Newfoundland which is so vital a part of the defence of the continent and the hemisphere. They hope that the people of Newfoundland will find some wholly satisfactory solution of the political and economic problems which confront them. They will be happy if, in any way, they can contribute to the solution of these problems, many of which are common to both countries.
If the people of Newfoundland should ever decide that they wish to enter the Canadian federation and should make that decision clear beyond all possibility of misunderstanding, Canada would give most sympathetic consideration to the proposal.

Mr. Chairman, I
wish to say this to the Prime Minister with respect to what he said a minute ago regarding the Chinese. So far as the remarks being repeated in China and having an effect upon the Chinese feelings are concerned, I would say that the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would be exactly of the kind that would greatly disturb these people. Why the Prime Minister should limit the discussion when I asked a question in an endeavour to arrive at some definite indication of what the first lady of China did request, I really cannot see. I do not know why the Prime Minister should object to that question, but if he does, then we shall pass it by. However, I should like to point out to the Prime Minister that I have sat in this house for seven years, and it is simply astounding to me how many problems are like the one the Prime Minister mentioned a moment ago. I know this is a question that is of vital concern to the country, and hon. members want to discuss it. When one tries to get something definite the Prime Minister finds some reason or another for deferring the discussion. For example, he said it was highly inflammatory to discuss sending materials to Japan, about which the Chinese now complain- bitterly. If we discussed this matter before the Japanese entered the war or even before there was a war, we were told we might offend the Japanese and cause much trouble. Now, you see what happened. Instead of the house coming to some sort of definite conclusion, and the government telling the house frankly in private session, if needs be, we just let things drift. A similar thing has happened with respect to the Japanese. I am not making a pronouncement on the question of the Japanese at this time, nor do I propose to do so. But as I said on Friday, I have an idea as to how the matter should be taken care of. And it was partly because of that idea that I asked the Prime Minister a question about China.
We started many years ago to make representations with respect to the Japanese. Hon. members from British Columbia have been here to Ottawa, doing everything in their mortal power to arouse Ottawa-and with just a hundred per cent failure. The result is that the people of British Columbia have been suffering a serious injustice and have been led to feel in a way that no province in Canada should be forced to feel. And still the problem is unsolved. If we go on at our present rate, or the rate we have taken in the last twenty years, it will be unsolved

War Appropriation-External Affairs
seven hundred years from to-day. Surely the time should come when we might discuss these matters to a conclusion, and get somewhere.
As I said, I am not going to urge this matter upon the Prime Minister. But I am telling him how I feel about deferring the discussion of a good many of these matters. I referred on Friday night to a problem facing us in Alberta, one which is rapidly growing worse. If it continues for another forty or fifty years, it will probably reach the point where it will be beyond solution. There may be bloodshed as a result of it. Yet we can get no help at all from Ottawa. Ottawa brought the people into the country, planted them on our doorstep, went away and said, "Now it is up to you." And every move we make to solve the problem Ottawa says, "No, no, you must not do that; naughty, naughty; spank your hands!" Well, if we think that is the way to run a country like Canada, then I say our opinions are open to some considerable revision. In a general way I believe I have delivered myself of my thoughts along that line.
I should like for a moment to revert to the remarks of the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) in connection with this matter of the British empire. Friday and to-day we have heard much discussion regarding Canada's relationship with the British empire. Although I have listened with most attentive care, I have not been able to arrive at a clear conception of what hon. members have in mind. I thought the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) was trying to read a lecture to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) because of some remarks he had made in support of the British empire. When I examined with great care the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, as reported in Hansard, I found it very difficult to find any difference between the two of them. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George will not go far enough to say he wishes to cut this country right out of the empire. He arose much disturbed this afternoon because it had been suggested in the remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George was an isolationist. Well, where does he stand? And where do these men who believe as he believes stand? What do they want?
I would ask the Prime Minister two or three questions, to see whether he can enlighten us, or whether he will say that this is a problem which ought not to be discussed
in war time. Is he prepared to accept the remarks of the Right Hon. Anthony Eden, as reported, that the British commonwealth of nations is a blueprint of the future organization of the nations of the world, or that it is a blueprint or a new order for the new organization of nations.
Before the Prime Minister answers, may I point out to him that there are a number of us who are at a loss to know what was in the minds of hon. members when they talked about supranational governments. I say the house ought to have clearly in mind just exactly what the government proposes. If needs be, it should be given us in a secret session. But, above all, surely members of parliament ought to know exactly what the government has in mind, and what it means when it uses a certain phrase.
I was much pleased when the Right Hon. Anthony Eden said that the British commonwealth of nations was a blueprint of the new organization of the nations of the world. Perhaps the Prime Minister will tell me whether I was misinformed regarding Mr. Eden's remarks, and whether he agrees with Mr. Eden in that regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not sure what Mr. Eden meant by a blueprint. He might have one thing in mind, and I might have another. However, I always have felt the British commonwealth of nations was certainly a pattern on which the world might well seek to organize itself. It would be a community of nations, all of which gained a measure of mutual security through belonging to one great entity such as the commonwealth of nations. If to-morrow Canada were to be out of the British commonwealth of nations, she would have to find some nations with which she would wish to be associated sufficiently closely to find security in that association. And I think in all probability she would return immediately to the group with which at the moment she is associated, because I doubt if there could be a better group. I should like to see that pattern extended. I think it would mean everything to the world if it could be so organized that all countries were free and independent, in a position to cooperate freely with each other, held together by a common bond of allegiance to a crown, representative of sovereignty, such as we give to our sovereign to-day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, we are not finished yet. It is just as well not to put on pressure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the committee has reached the stage where we cannot much longer permit repetition. It is a fact that there is no rule precluding repetition in committee. However, I have in mind the discussion on the Japanese question, a matter which has been before us on four other occasions, and I would ask some hon. members not to repeat what they have said many times before.

Mr. Chairman, I believe I am not repeating what has already been said. I am merely seeking clarification. The reply of the Prime Minister, as nearly as I could judge from listening to him, would be exactly the concept most hon. members on this side of the house would have. I believe that would be exactly the concept of Social Credit-ers, and I am almost positive it would be the concept of the Progressive Conservative party. That being so, then why all the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George who seemed to be endeavouring to indicate a trace of difference between his point of view and that of hon. members opposite? You see, the reply by the Prime Minister deprives the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George of any sense. There is no question about that. I wonder if the hon. member for Swift Current will agree entirely with what the Prime Minister has said. And if he does, then how can he agree entirely with what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has said?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: There was no difference.

If there is no difference between what was said by the Prime Minister and what was said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, then evidently the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George was trying to make a distinction without a difference. I note that the hon. member for Swift Current shakes his head; evidently there is still some confusion in his mind.
I say that in discussing Canada's foreign policy this matter ought to be cleared up. If the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, notwithstanding all that has been said, can see any difference between his point of view and that of the hon. member for Lethbridge, then I think he should explain so that the hon. member for Lethbridge can understand. I do not think I-
Carried.

No; it is not carried, and I can tell hon. members that calling out "carried" is not going to carry this item one minute sooner. In fact, it is likely to take a good deal longer. Let us have that perfectly clear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member for Lethbridge that he has no right to use threats. I believe it is the wish of the committee that there should be no repetition and also that these items should go through as soon as possible.

There is no doubt that they would like .to see the items passed, and so would I. But I want to have certain matters cleared up. Does the Prime Minister believe that to-day Canada has all the autonomy under the British empire that she should have? Is there room for her to increase her autonomy under the British empire?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend means by autonomy under the British empire.
Within the British empire.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Within the British empire I think Canada has just as much autonomy as has the United Kingdom. I believe we are masters of our own house in all particulars, with relation to both our domestic and external affairs. As compared one to the other, we are all equal in status and united by a common allegiance to the crown.

That is most enlightening, because I have gathered from the remarks of three or four members who have spoken that they can see that as a result of this war Canada is going to go forward to some fuller measure of nationhood than she had before. I have heard hon. members state outside the house-they have not said it inside the house-that the fact that Canada had declared war in her own right was a step forward in the development of the autonomy of Canada. In other words, before Canada declared war in 1939, Canada did not possess the autonomy that she would dream of possessing, or the autonomy which she will possess from now on. That, of course, takes the point from the Prime Minister's answer, and it will be seen why there is confusion in these matters. If I am wrong, I should be glad to be put right on the matter.

Item agreed to.
Representation abroad, $111,500.

About three weeks ago I made an inquiry of the government based upon a report from Stockholm, Sweden, to the effect that some representation to Canada was in contemplation by the Swedish government. At the time the Prime Minister

War Appropriation-External Affairs
answered that so far as Canada was concerned there had been no intimation officially between the two governments, and I was wondering if there had been any change in the situation since that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Since my hon. friend asked me that question the Swedish consul general at Montreal called upon me and intimated that the government of Sweden would like to appoint a mission to Canada and wished to know whether it would be agreeable to our country to have a Swedish legation opened here and whether we would reciprocate. I outlined to the Swedish consul general, as I have to the house, the difficulties we were confronted with in the matter of personnel required for legations abroad and that we had hoped before this year to have opened a legation in Mexico and in one or two other countries. I told him I could not give an assurance that a legation would be opened immediately in Sweden, but we would be prepared to receive a mission here on the understanding that later on we would reciprocate, but that we might find it desirable to have a charge d'affaires in charge of our legation in Sweden in the first instance rather than a minister.
Are there any exchanges of diplomatic representatives under consideration in addition to those mentioned already by the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In these matters that relate to the representation of different countries the practice more or less followed is not to disclose in advance the intentions of the government. Possibly I had better not attempt to say more than that we do expect in the course of time to open additional legations.
Can the minister tell us in a general way, with some detail, what are the duties of the legations for which we are paying under this vote? Choose any one at random and tell us what its duties are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The report of the Department of External Affairs gives rather full particulars of the services which the different legations have rendered. Perhaps my hon. friend would allow me to refer him to that report. I think he will get full particulars there.
Does that mean that we cannot have the answer to this question appear in Hansard?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When the full particulars are in a government report, when I have given my hon. friend the information
in a form that can be referred to, why should he wish to have it placed on Hansard? It is not going to alter the business of the legations in the least if the information with regard to them is given in a report rather than in Hansard.
Is it not the right of members when they are being asked to provide money to ask what the money is being spent for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have referred my hon. friend to a report which will give him the full particulars. I think I am quite within my rights, and indeed I am only helping to conserve- the money of the country by referring my hon. friend to a report which will give him full particulars, instead of placing the report on Hansard as he suggests.

If every minister replied as the Prime Minister has done, by referring the questioner to reference books and reports, there would be an end of the examination of the minister in committee by members of parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the year ended December 31, 1942, was prepared in order that hon. members might be fully informed in advance of any discussion of the duties and responsibilities of the officials who are connected with the legations and of the services performed by the legations. I submit that my hon. friend is asking a question which in the circumstances is wholly unnecessary. He knows in a general way that the business of a legation is to carry on official dealings and relations with governments of other countries in connection with the questions that may arise or are of interest and concern between them. Where there is public business to be carried out, it is carried out by means of diplomats who serve as officials of legations. What the details of that business may be, I cannot begin to go into at the moment.
In view of the war being in its fourth year, I think this might well be an off year in the appointing of foreign representatives.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would suggest to the hon. member for Broadview that this matter has been discussed several times already. I do not think the members of the committee are in a mood to have a repetition of discussion.

As I understand it, this
item covers representation abroad, $111,500. I was going to suggest that in the interests of economy no appointments should be made

War Appropriation-External Affairs
during this fiscal year. Several of these representatives have been appointed, and I have always been opposed to such appointments because they duplicate the work of our trade commissioners. They also duplicate the work of the British representatives in the different countries. These appointments cause divisions. I suggest that now we have gone pretty nearly far enough. I read to-day the speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. If this is the policy of the government, to appoint ambassadors over the seven seas, new representatives here, there, and everywhere, we might just as well get out of the British empire altogether. We have no representative in one fine country to which Mr. Churchill referred the other day, and which may be appropriately mentioned to-day. I refer to Ulster. Ulster has no direct representation in this country, nor we in hers, but we might well recall the great tribute paid a few days ago by the Prime Minister of Britain to that little country which is never mentioned here.
I suggest that in the interests of harmony in the British empire we suspend any more appointments of representatives abroad. There are one or two of them in Toronto. One of them, the representative of China, -was most insulting to the city of Toronto. He went to New York, and from there to China, and1 allow me to say that if he causes as much division in China as he caused in Toronto he is no fit representative of this country. He has not the training. How are these ministers and others appointed? What is their background? Have they ever had any training in diplomacy? I doubt if our representative who went to China knows enough Chinese to walk into any office over there and carry on a conversation with the Chinese. We are just duplicating our representatives abroad, making believe that we are a separate state when we are not. We are part and parcel of the British empire. There is no point in multiplying our representatives abroad and indulging in all these forms of what I call separatism, particularly in time of war. It is bad enough in peace time, but even more disastrous in war time. I suggest that in this direction we take a holiday in the coming year. We have pretty'well covered the seven seas already with our representatives, and I do not know any other place we can send them to at the present time. I sincerely hope that in the interests of economy there will be a cessation of appointments of ministers plenipotentiary and envoys extraordinary-and I can tell you a whole lot of them are extraordinary.
